❯ Can you help me create an web interactive 6502 disassembler taking            
  inspiration from my CLI disassembler located in ../dis?  The main idea is to  
  have a live dissassembly of the loaded binary on screen that the user can     
  interact with in real time. So, for example, every time they add a new label, 
  the disassembly updates immediately. Or every time they mark a section of     
  memory as code/data, for example, the disassembly immediately reflects that   
  change. The web page should provide a way to load binary data to be           
  disassembled and load/save project info and save the generated assembly code.

● Found two bugs: XEX detection was misfiring on files starting with $FF $FF
  like esmc.bin, and MADS rejects xasm's a: prefix syntax. I'll make XEX
  detection require full valid parsing before matching, and add an explicit
  syntax option (xasm/mads) so MADS gets proper headers and the .a mnemonic
  suffix.

● I've built xdis, a web-based interactive version of your dis disassembler, in
  /home/lybrown/x/xdis. Open index.html in a browser; there's no build step.
  Nothing is committed yet.

  Testing: across 13 test cases (your escm project, ransack, bomber, boink, two
  SAP files, a C64 PRG, raw dumps, and projects with every kind of edit
  applied), the exported .asm reassembles with xasm.exe or mads into a file
  identical to the original. On every file the CLI can also handle, it finds
  exactly the same code as dis. I also ran 40 other XEX/OBX files from ~/x
  through the same check and all 40 came back identical. A scripted test that
  drives the actual page in headless Chrome (rename, mark data, undo/redo,
  comments, goto, constants, pointer tables, the right-click menu, saving and
  reloading) passes reliably.

  How it works:
  - Live updates: every change re-runs the full trace and redraws the listing.
    Ransack (51K bytes, 6,800 lines) takes about 50 ms.
  - Keys: C marks code, D/T/W mark data/text/words, A/P mark pointer tables, V
    marks a vector, U undoes a marking, N names, ; comments, G is goto, Enter
    follows an operand and Esc goes back. There's also undo/redo, a right-click
    menu, and a side panel showing callers and accessors.
  - Memory map: a strip above the listing that you can click to jump around.
  - Loading: raw files (with a load address), XEX/COM, SAP and PRG, by button or
    drag-and-drop. You can also pass files in the URL when serving it over http
    (?bin=…&dop=…).
  - Saving:
    - Save .asm writes exactly what's on screen.
    - Save project writes an .xdis.json file, with the binary inside it by
      default.
    - Export .dop writes an option file your CLI can read. Things only the web
      version knows about (comments, text formatting, etc.) go in ;xdis comment
      lines, which dis ignores and xdis reads back.
    - Import .dop loads your existing option files.
    - The session also autosaves in the browser.
  - Symbol files: your hardware, sys, vic, sid, cia and 6510 .dop files are
    built in and can be switched on with one click.
  - Assembler output: choose xasm or MADS. MADS rejects the CLI's org f: and a:,
    so in MADS mode segment headers are written out explicitly and .a replaces
    a:.

  Where it differs from dis, all listed in the README:
  - Data is grouped 8 bytes per line, and long runs of one byte collapse to a
    single repeat line. Your escm $FF fill becomes :6144 dta $FF, so the Perl
    cleanup step in that Makefile isn't needed.
  - A single name inside a named data range now wins instead of being dropped as
    a duplicate (dlistjvb now gets its own label).

  Two bugs this found in dis itself, both fixed in xdis but not in the CLI:
  - xasm silently merges a segment into the one right before it when they're
    back-to-back in memory. That's why dis can't round-trip Lasermania.sap.
  - Truncated XEX files (like bomber/title.xex) lose their original segment
    header.

  Testing setup: the tests use a Node binary I downloaded into .cache/
  (git-ignored, about 100 MB, safe to delete). The test binaries come from
  neighbouring folders like ../escm and ../ransack; any that are missing are
  skipped.

  Code is in js/core.js (the disassembly logic, which also runs under Node) and
  js/app.js (the page). The README covers usage, keys, file formats and how to
  run the tests.

● All four requests are in. The disassembly round-trip tests still produce
  byte-identical output in all 13 cases, and the UI test suite (now 40 checks)
  passes every time. None of this is committed yet.

  1. Labels on bytes inside a dta line. Click any byte to pick it: in the dta
  operands, a single character of a c'…' string, or the raw bytes column (which
  also works on instruction operand bytes, handy for self-modifying code).
  Left/Right arrow keys step through the bytes of a line. The picked byte is
  outlined, and the address column, status bar ("byte 4 of 8") and inspector all
  show it. Then:
  - N names that byte; double-clicking a byte does the same in one step. The dta
    line splits so the label sits right before the byte, and the cursor stays
    on it.
  - ;, :, C, D, T, W, A and the other keys apply to that one byte too.
  - Exception: a collapsed :N dta $XX fill run can only be picked as a whole.

  2. Editing directives. Each directive in the Directives panel and in the
  inspector's "Directives here" list now has a ✎ button; double-clicking it
  works too. It turns into a text field in the usual option-file form, such as
  code start=$2000 or data tbl=$3000+FF. Enter applies and the disassembly
  updates; Escape cancels. Invalid text is rejected with a message and the field
  stays open. You can change the type, name, address or range this way, e.g.
  switch data to text.

  3. Memory map. The bug was in caching. After each edit, the view cached the
  old map image (old colors and the old white viewport box) as its clean
  background, then pasted it over the freshly drawn map. Now the clean image is
  saved only right after a full repaint, so colors follow your edits and only
  the current viewport box is shown. I confirmed this with screenshots taken
  after a series of edits and scrolls.

  4. Map dragging outside the strip. A click-drag on the map now keeps tracking
  the mouse anywhere on screen. Past the left or right end it stops at the first
  or last byte, and gaps between segments snap to the nearest one.

  Your main branch has no upstream yet, so it looks like the first push hasn't
  happened. Do you want me to commit these changes so they go up together with
  the initial commit?

● Clicking a problem now takes you to where it applies. Clickable problems
  highlight on hover, and the tooltip says where the click goes.

  - Label defined twice: jumps to the second definition (e.g. $3C65).
  - Trace problems: an instruction running past the end of memory, or an
    indirect JMP through undefined memory, jumps to that instruction.
  - Truncated XEX segments: jumps to the start of the segment.
  - Pointer or vector into unloaded memory: jumps to the address if any part of
    it is loaded. Otherwise it opens the Directives panel filtered to the
    directive that caused it.
  - Directives with a bad segment or out-of-range address: opens the Directives
    panel filtered to that directive, ready to edit with ✎.
  - Corrupted XEX tail: jumps to the ; Corrupted segment block.
  - Not clickable: .dop import errors only have a file and line number, so they
    stay plain text.

  Each jump is added to the back history, so Esc returns.

  I added a UI test that creates a duplicate label and a directive with a bad
  segment, clicks both problems, checks where each lands, then undoes the
  changes. The full UI suite passes on repeated runs, and the round-trip tests
  still produce byte-identical output in all 13 cases. I also added a line about
  it to the README.

● The Directives pane now tags every directive that isn't needed to get the
  current split between code and data.

  What you'll see:
  - "no effect" (amber): an unnamed code or data directive that changes nothing.
  - "name only": a named code or data directive. Tracing would reach it anyway;
    it only supplies the name, which a plain label would also do.
  - "format only": a text, word, vector, address or codeptr directive that only
    changes how the bytes are shown.

  The header reads, for example, "Directives (121) · 119 not needed for
  tracing", or shows progress while checking. A new checkbox, Only show 
  directives not needed for tracing, filters the list to the tagged ones. The
  inspector's "Directives here" list shows the same tags. Symbol-set directives
  aren't checked, since you can't delete them individually.

  One design decision you should know about: checked one at a time, directives
  can hide each other. In your esmc project, code cartstart=$B800 and vector 
  CARTSTARTVEC=$BFFA each make the other look removable, but removing both loses
  the entry point. So the check is cumulative: each directive is tested with
  all the already-tagged ones removed too. That means everything tagged can be
  deleted together safely. It also means only one of such a pair gets tagged.
  Unnamed directives are tried first and vectors and pointers last, so the
  vector is the one kept. For esmc, 119 of 121 are tagged; only code setrunad
  and vector CARTSTARTVEC are needed for tracing.

  How it runs: after each edit it re-runs the analysis without each candidate,
  in small background chunks. Directives that only touch unloaded memory are
  decided instantly. esmc's full check takes about 50 ms, and an edit made
  mid-check restarts it.

  Testing:
  - Round-trip suite: every case with directives now also deletes all tagged
    directives together and confirms the traced code is identical. That holds in
    all of them, and the output is still byte-identical in all 13 cases.
  - UI suite: checks that an extra code entry on an already-traced instruction
    is tagged "no effect", that a needed one isn't, and that the filter, tags
    and count render. It passes on repeated runs.
  - Bug found and fixed: a screenshot showed the tags were missing if the check
    finished while another tab was open. The list now refreshes when you open
    the Directives tab.

● Found that xasm keeps relocated bytes inline with run addresses, while MADS's

● Here's what I found and how I'd approach it. I ran small experiments with your
  xasm.exe and mads.

  What org r: actually does (from xasm's source)

  xasm keeps two counters:
  - origin: where code is assembled, i.e. the value of * and of labels.
  - loadOrigin: where bytes land in the file.

  org r:$30 sets only origin, so the bytes stay inline in the same load block. A
  later plain org at the next load address continues the same block without a
  new header. It works with opt h- too.

  MADS equivalent: org $30,*. Under opt h-, which xdis's MADS output already
  uses, it emits no header. Both assemblers reproduced my test bytes exactly.

  One real hazard: without z:, xasm assembled a forward reference to a zero-page
  label as absolute (ad 36 00 instead of a5 35). That shifts every later byte.
  MADS handled it because it takes more passes. Code relocated to zero page is a
  prime use case, so xdis would need to emit z: on forward zero-page references
  in xasm mode.

  How it could fit xdis

  1. New directive: relocate, e.g. relocate code_zpage=$8013+5 $30, meaning
  "bytes loaded at $8013–$8018 run at $0030".
  - It would round-trip through .dop files as a ;xdis line, like the other
    extensions.
  - The dis CLI could take it as an option later.

  2. Model a relocated block as a sub-segment. xdis already handles overlaid XEX
  segments, so this reuses that machinery.
  - Analysis: split the parent segment into before / relocated / after pieces.
    The relocated piece's "start" is the run address and it remembers its load
    address. Tracing, labels, cross-references and memory classes then work in
    run addresses with no special cases. jmp code_zpage from the loader resolves
    to the block, and branches inside the block land on run addresses.
  - Load range becomes a hole: labels can't be defined inside org r: code and
    still mean load addresses. So the load range becomes a gap in the parent.
    References into it (the copy loop's lda code_loaded,x) become equ 
    $8013-style externs, or code_loaded+N.
  - The label exactly at the load start can be defined inline just before the
    org r: line, because * is still the load address there. That's precisely how
    xasm's own manual example does it.
  - Numbering: give pieces indices after the real segments. That keeps
    3:2000-style segment-qualified directives stable when relocations are added
    or removed.

  3. Output.
  - xasm: org r:$30 before the block, then a plain org $<load end+1> after it,
    plus the z: fix above.
  - MADS: org $30,*, then org $<load end+1>.
  - I'd extend the round-trip tests with a synthetic relocated file and a
    cartridge that copies code to RAM.

  4. UI.
  - Relocate… (R) on a selection, prompting for the run address.
  - Address column: show the run address, with the load address shown dimmed or
    in the inspector ("loaded at $8013, runs at $0030").
  - Memory map: hatch relocated pieces.
  - Go to: a load address inside a relocated block jumps to its line.

  5. Detection. xdis could also find relocations itself and suggest them:
  - Copy loops: lda L,x / sta R,x / dex / bpl (the expansion of mva:rpl), with
    the length taken from the preceding ldx #n (bne/dey variants too). That
    gives L, R and the length directly.
  - Unloaded jump targets: a trace that jumps or calls into unloaded memory
    (especially zero page or $0600), where a candidate block decodes cleanly at
    that base.
  - Presentation: these would show up as clickable suggestions in Problems
    ("Code copied from $8013 to $0030 — relocate?").

  Open questions

  - Several copies: if the same block is copied to more than one place, one
    mapping per block is simplest. Is that enough?
  - Overlap: a relocated block whose run range overlaps a real segment works
    through the overlay machinery. Labels there would get s14l0030-style names.
  - Large copies: page-copy loops (incrementing the high bytes) and MVSB-style
    macros are harder to detect than the simple pattern above.

  The z: forward-reference fix is worth doing regardless, since it already
  affects any program that defines zero-page labels inline. Do you want me to
  implement this, starting with the directive, the sub-segment model and the
  output?

  described: the code loaded at $5600 is disassembled at $A000, and the output
  still reassembles byte-for-byte with both xasm and MADS.

  What happens when you open the example:
  - Suggestion: the status bar says "1 relocated code block found — see
    Problems". The entry there says code at $5600–$75FF is copied to $A000 by
    the loop at $5531, and that's exactly the relocate 7:$5600+1FFF $A000 you
    described.
  - Applying it: clicking it opens a prefilled dialog. Confirming disassembles
    the block at $A000–$BFFF. In the listing, org r:$A000 sits right after the
    loader code, jmp lA000 from the loader lands inside the block, and
    callers/branches use run addresses.
  - Your directives move with it: code 7:$582E becomes code $A22E, and data 
    $6A3C+1 becomes data $B43C+1. Removing the relocation moves them back.

  Using it on other files:
  - Manually: select the code and press R (also in the right-click menu), or
    type relocate $5600+1FFF $A000 in the Directives panel. Pressing R inside a
    relocated block offers to remove it, as do the inspector button and deleting
    the directive.
  - Inspector: shows "relocated block (from 7)" and the load address. Hovering
    over a relocated block's address column shows its load address too.
  - Segment table and memory map: the block is listed under its segment, and the
    map draws it where it's loaded, with a teal stripe.
  - Go to: go to $6344 or 7:$582E and you land on the matching run address.
  - Output: xasm gets org r:$A000, then a plain org back to the load address
    after the block if more of the segment follows. MADS gets org $A000,*.
  - Saving: projects and .dop exports keep the relocation. In .dop files it's an
    ;xdis relocate … line, which dis ignores.
  - Detection: finds lda src,x / sta dst,x / dex / bpl|bne loops, and page
    copies through zero-page pointers (your Galaxian loop). It only suggests
    copies whose destination is later called or jumped to, so plain data copies
    aren't flagged.

  Also fixed along the way:
  - z: prefix: xasm output now adds z: on forward references to zero-page
    labels. Without it, xasm assembles them as absolute and every later byte
    shifts; this mostly matters for code relocated to zero page. dis has the
    same issue.
  - Dialog bug: the tests found that dialogs occasionally didn't take effect
    after clicking OK. Dialogs now act on the button press directly, which
    removed the flakiness.

  Testing:
  - Round trips: three new cases (Galaxian with xasm and with MADS, the
    zero-page forward reference, and a synthetic indexed copy loop). All 17
    cases are byte-identical.
  - UI suite: a relocation section clicks the suggestion, applies it, checks the
    listing, inspector and go-to, then removes it and checks the directives
    move back. It passes on repeated runs.

❯ In Galaxian, I'd like to emit the operand of the lda instruction at A392 as

● We support this already, with the address directive in its split hi/lo form.
  Before telling you exactly what to type, let me look at the code around $A392
  in the relocated project:

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● Yes, this is already supported: it's the address directive in its split form,
  HI_LO. Each half names the address of one operand byte. The high byte is the
  operand of lda at $A392, so it's at $A393; the low byte is at $A397:

  address $A393_A397

  I tried it on your relocated Galaxian project and it gives:

      lda #>lBA45               ; A392: A9 BA
      sta INSDAT                ; A394: 85 7D
      lda #<lBA45               ; A396: A9 45
      sta vec           ; A398: 85 7C

  xdis writes it as #>lBA45 rather than >lBA45. Both xasm and MADS accept that
  form, and it reassembles to the same bytes.

  Since $BA45 is code reached through your vec vector, I'd use codeptr 
  $A393_A397 instead. It renders the same, but it also traces $BA45 as code.
  That makes your separate code entry for it unnecessary, and the Directives
  pane would tag that entry "no effect". Type either one into the Directives
  panel's add box. Use the run addresses as shown, since this code is in the
  relocated block.

  Automatic detection: yes, it's a good candidate, offered as suggestions in
  Problems like the relocations rather than applied silently. The pattern is:
  - lda #hi / sta P+1 and lda #lo / sta P close together, in either order,
    storing to adjacent bytes.
  - Also ldx #hi / ldy #lo (or similar register pairs) right before a jsr to a
    routine like SETVBV that takes an address that way.

  A lot of unrelated code stores two immediates to adjacent bytes (colors,
  counters), so I'd only suggest a pair when there's other evidence. Any of
  these would count:
  - P is used as a pointer: a vector directive (your vec), jmp (P), or (P),y /
    (P,x) addressing.
  - The combined address lands on traced code or an existing label.
  - The address falls inside loaded memory and isn't trivially small.

  Your case scores on the first two. A suggestion would read like "lda #$BA /
  lda #$45 at $A392 form $BA45 (stored into vec) — click to make them #>lBA45 /
  #<lBA45". It would pick codeptr when the target is code and address otherwise.

  One side note: sta INSDAT is really the high byte of your vec pointer. The OS
  name from sys.dop wins over vec+1, because an exact name beats an offset into
  a range.

  Want me to implement the detection?

❯ yes, implement the detection                                                  

● I'll build it in the core alongside the relocation detector, reusing its
  instruction scan, then surface the results as Problems suggestions.

  Detection rules:
  - Pattern: within one straight-line block, an immediate load (lda/ldx/ldy #)
    stored to P and another stored to P+1, in either order. Register-pair
    hand-offs (ldx #hi / ldy #lo / jsr …) count too.
  - Evidence required: either P is used as a pointer (a vector/pointer
    directive, jmp (P), (P),y, or (P,x)), or the combined address lands on
    traced code or an existing label.
  - Directive suggested: codeptr when the target is code (or P is a jump
    vector), otherwise address.

● Pointer detection works. In your Galaxian project, the pair at $A392/$A396
  shows up as a suggestion. Clicking it opens a preview of lda #>lBA45 / lda 
  #<lBA45, and Apply adds codeptr $A393_A397.

  How it decides: within one stretch of straight-line code, it looks for two
  immediate loads stored into adjacent bytes P and P+1, or handed to a
  subroutine in two registers (like SETVBV). It only suggests a pair when
  there's evidence it's an address:
  - P is a known word location: used as (P),y, (P,x) or jmp (P), a vector, or a
    2-byte range in a symbol set (SAVMSC=$58+1, VDSLST), or
  - the address lands on loaded code or a label.

  Stores to the I/O area are ignored, so pairs like HPOSP0/HPOSP1 or
  COLPF0/COLPF1 aren't flagged. Jump vectors become codeptr, and pointers used
  for data become address.

  Results on your files:
  - Galaxian: 38 suggestions: 12 code vectors (DOSINI, VDSLST, VVBLKI, VIMIRQ,
    your vec) and 26 data pointers for its memory clear and copy routines. The
    OS ones get names, e.g. #>COLDSV.
  - Others: bomber 8, ransack 1, boink 1.
  - Before tightening the rules there were 74 on Galaxian, mostly adjacent
    hardware registers; those are gone now.

  In the app:
  - Problems now has a separate teal count for suggestions next to the orange
    one for real problems.
  - An Apply all N pointer suggestions button applies them in one undoable step.
  - Each suggestion's dialog lets you switch between code pointer and data
    pointer before applying.
  - Opening a file reports something like "Found 1 relocated code block and 38
    likely pointers — see Problems".

  Testing:
  - Round trips: three new cases apply every suggestion (Galaxian under xasm and
    MADS, bomber). All 20 cases reassemble byte-identical.
  - UI suite: clicks your $A392 suggestion, checks both instructions, then uses
    Apply all. It passes on repeated runs.
  - Galaxian test copy: you'd already relocated the block in examples/, so the
    round-trip test now writes a copy without the relocation to test/out/ for
    the UI test to start from.

  Something odd in your edited example: it now has vector vechi=$7C and vector 
  veclo=$7D. A vector directive covers two bytes, so veclo=$7D treats $7D/$7E as
  a second pointer. Also, $7C is the low byte (the code stores #$45 there). If
  you just wanted names for the two halves, I'd use vector vec=$7C plus label 
  vechi=$7D.

  I documented the directive and the detection in the README. Want me to commit?

      dta a(cartinit)        ; BFFE: F2 BC

  A naming catch. Everything else in sys.dop uses uppercase OS names, and escm
  shows how lowercase names can collide. There, esmc.dop names the routine at
  $B800 cartstart, while the new sys.dop entry names the vector at $BFFA
  cartstart. It only works out because the project's own CARTSTARTVEC takes
  priority at $BFFA. A project that names its start routine cartstart but leaves
  the vector unnamed would end up with cartstart defined twice: Problems would
  flag it and the assembler would reject it.

  Atari's own names for these locations are CARTCS ($BFFA, start address), CART
  ($BFFC), CARTFG ($BFFD, flags) and CARTAD ($BFFE, init address). Using those
  avoids the clash, and you'd still be free to call your routines
  cartstart/cartinit.

  Do you want me to switch to the Atari names, and/or add the same lines to
  ../dis/sys.dop so the CLI matches? Either way, say when to commit.

● I've switched to Atari's names. With sys.dop enabled, every cartridge header
  is now labeled and traced automatically. On the escm cart, with no project
  directives at all, it finds 603 of the 609 instructions that your hand-built
  esmc.dop reaches:

  CARTCS
      dta a(lB800)              ; BFFA: 00 B8
  CART
      dta $00           ; BFFC: 00
  CARTFG
      dta $04           ; BFFD: 04
  CARTAD
      dta a(lBCF2)              ; BFFE: F2 BC

  CART and CARTFG are data, so they also stop tracing from running into the
  header bytes. js/symbols.js is regenerated, and all 20 round-trip cases still
  pass. Not committed yet, and ../dis/sys.dop is unchanged.

  Where the names came from: from memory at first; they're the standard OS
  equates from Mapping the Atari and Atari's OS listing. I then checked them
  against cc65's asminc/atari.inc in your ~/x/cc65 checkout, which has all four
  at the same addresses. That file, plus atari_antic.inc, atari_gtia.inc and
  atari_pokey.inc, is a good source to harvest more from. cc65 is zlib-licensed,
  so reusing the equates with credit is fine.

  What a harvest would add: cc65 defines 621 equates. 341 of the names aren't in
  our .dop files, and 178 of those are at addresses we have no label for at
  all. It isn't a straight merge, though:
  - OS ROM entry points (about 32): the floating-point package (AFP $D800, FASC,
    IFP, FPI, ZFR0, …) and parallel bus vectors. These are worth having.
  - XL/XE OS additions: page-2/3 locations marked ##rev2## (VPIRQ $0238, PDIMSK,
    KEYDIS, …). Also worth having.
  - Locations that moved between OS revisions: 14 names disagree with your
    sys.dop (PTIMOT is $1C there but $0314 in cc65, likewise PBPNT, CRETRY,
    CKEY, …). Your sys.dop follows the original 400/800 OS, while cc65 follows
    the XL/XE OS.
  - Not addresses or not OS: KEY_* keyboard codes (values that would look like
    zero-page labels if read as addresses), Atari BASIC's zero page (LOMEM,
    VNTP, …), and DOS/SpartaDOS locations (DOS $0700, SDX_VERSION).

  What I'd suggest: rather than growing sys.dop, add separate symbol sets you
  can switch on per program:
  - atarixl.dop: XL/XE OS additions, and the relocated locations using cc65's
    addresses.
  - atarifp.dop: the floating-point ROM routines and their zero-page registers.
  - basic.dop and dos.dop, if you disassemble BASIC or DOS-related code.

  KEY_* codes I'd leave out, since they aren't addresses.

  Want me to generate those sets from cc65 (with a small regeneration script,
  like embed-symbols.py)? And should I commit the cartridge names now, and copy
  them to ../dis/sys.dop too?

● I generated the new symbol sets and committed everything as ee5445c; nothing
  is left uncommitted. All 25 round-trip cases reassemble byte-identical, and
  the UI suite passes.

  Cartridge header: sys.dop now names it CARTCS ($BFFA), CART ($BFFC), CARTFG
  ($BFFD) and CARTAD ($BFFE). Any cartridge image now traces from its header on
  its own; escm finds 603 of its 609 instructions without its own .dop.

  New symbol sets (four .dop files, 153 entries in total). They're generated
  from cc65's asminc/atari.inc by tools/harvest-cc65.py:
  - atarixl.dop: what the 1200XL and XL/XE OS added or moved (PTIMOT at $0314
    instead of $1C, VPIRQ, PDIMSK, the parallel device vectors, …), plus three
    OS equates sys.dop lacked.
  - atarifp.dop: the floating-point registers (FR0, FR1, …), buffers, and ROM
    routines (AFP, FASC, IFP, FADD, …).
  - basic.dop: Atari BASIC's zero page and its SIN/COS/ATAN/SQR routines.
  - dos.dop: DOS and the SpartaDOS X entry points.

  What the generator does:
  - Type and size of each entry come from cc65's comments, e.g. "2-byte …
    vector" becomes a vector, and FP/ROM routines become code.
  - Skipped: constants such as KEY_*, command codes, status codes and ATASCII,
    plus anything sys.dop/hardware.dop already label.
  - Not included: cc65's separate atari_gtia/pokey/antic register files. Every
    register in them is already in hardware.dop.

  Changes so the sets work together:
  - Priority: your own imported .dop files come first, then atarixl.dop, then
    hardware.dop, sys.dop and the rest. If two sets use the same name, only the
    first defines it, so turning on atarixl.dop puts XL addresses in place of
    the 400/800 ones without duplicate labels.
  - Panel layout: the Directives panel has new groups. Opening an Atari file
    still suggests only hardware.dop + sys.dop; the new sets are opt-in.
  - Refresh: built-in sets now update to the current text whenever a project
    loads. Your newest example had saved my short-lived lowercase cartstart
    lines in its sys.dop; it now picks up the Atari names. Files you import
    yourself keep their saved text.
  - Tests: every project in examples/ is now round-tripped, so both of your
    Galaxian projects are covered. There are also cases with all six Atari sets
    enabled.

  For your new Galaxian project: its own vector cartstart=$BFFA+1 and vector 
  cartinit=$BFFE+1 still take priority over CARTCS/CARTAD. If you're happy with
  Atari's names, you can delete them; tracing is the same either way.

  ../dis/sys.dop is still untouched; say if you want the cartridge names there
  too.

● Not cleanly, no. Two things go wrong with what you tried.

  Why address $0_4801 doesn't work. The split form needs both halves of the
  address to exist as bytes in the binary, high byte first: HI_LO. So $0_4801
  means "the high byte is at $0000 and the low byte is at $4801". $0000 isn't
  loaded, which is the warning you'd see in Problems ("pointer at $4801 is in
  undefined memory"). Here, though, there is no low byte anywhere. PMBASE only
  takes a page number, so the code only ever loads #$43.

  The closest thing today almost works. operand $4800 #>pmdata (the O key)
  renders lda #>pmdata. But because $4300 isn't loaded and the override text
  isn't treated as a reference, xdis never emits pmdata equ $4300. The saved
  .asm wouldn't assemble.

  Here's what I'd add:

  1. High-byte and low-byte directives, for when only one half of an address is
     in the code:
  hi $4801              ; operand byte $43 is the high byte of $4300 → #>pmdata
  hi $4801 $4380        ; ... of a specific address, if the label isn't 
  page-aligned
  lo $4805 $4380        ; low-byte-only counterpart (the target must be given)
     - Each renders #>label/#<label (or dta >label in data), names auto labels
       like l4300 when there's no user label, and makes sure the equ gets
       emitted.
     - A target that doesn't match the byte would show up in Problems.
     - The inspector would get a quick action for an instruction with an
       immediate operand.
  2. Operand overrides count as references. Labels mentioned in override text
     would get their equ emitted like any other reference. That fixes the trap
     above for every hand-written override.
  3. Detection, the same way as pointer pairs. Immediates stored into Atari's
     page registers (PMBASE, CHBASE/CHBAS, …) would be suggested as hi when that
     page is loaded or has a label. For Galaxian that would find your $4800
     case on its own, though only once you've labeled $4300, since that page
     isn't loaded.

  Want all three, or just the first two?

● All three are in and committed as 48cc2bd; nothing is left uncommitted. For
  your $4800, add data pmdata=$4300, then do any one of:
  - type hi $4801 in the Directives panel;
  - put the cursor on $4800 and press > (it prefills $4300; Enter applies);
  - accept the suggestion that now appears in Problems: "#$43 at $4800 stored
    into PMBASE is the page of $4300".

  The result is lda #>pmdata, with pmdata equ $4300 emitted, and it reassembles
  byte-identical.

  What's new:
  1. hi / lo directives:
     - Forms: hi $4801 means the byte is the high byte of $XX00. hi $4801 $4380
       names a specific address. lo $4805 $4380 needs the full address, since
       the high byte isn't in the code.
     - Output: #>label / #<label on immediates, or dta >label in data. When
       there's no label at the target, an automatic one like l4300 is used. A
       target that doesn't match the byte shows up in Problems.
     - In the UI: the > and < keys, buttons in the inspector for immediate
       instructions, and context-menu entries. They work on a picked byte too,
       and on a label line they apply to the instruction it labels.
  2. Operand overrides count as references. Labels named in an override
     (including auto names like l4300) now get their equ emitted, so operand 
     $4800 #>pmdata produces source that assembles.
  3. Page-register detection (Atari files only): an immediate stored into
     PMBASE, CHBASE or CHBAS is suggested as hi when that page is loaded or has
     a label. In Galaxian it found two CHBASE stores pointing at character sets
     (#>l3A00, #>l3000), plus your PMBASE store once pmdata exists. DLISTL and
     SDLSTL now also count as pointers for the pair detection.

  A bug the tests caught: with Galaxian's overlapping segments, a global
  directive placed where segment 5 overlaps segment 7's relocated block (e.g. hi
  $6219) was wrongly moved into the block at $AC19. A global directive now only
  moves into a block when no other segment loads that address.

  Testing:
  - Round trips: two new cases (Galaxian with page suggestions applied, and an
    operand-override case). All 27 cases reassemble byte-identical.
  - UI suite: > on $4800 prefills $4300 and gives #>l4300, then #>pmdata with
    its equ once the label is added. It passes on repeated runs.

  The README documents the directives and the detection. There are now 10 local
  commits, none pushed yet.

● The writes into the self-modifying jmp at $55AB can now be marked properly.
  Two of the steps already worked with existing directives; the third needed new
  detection, plus some fixes along the way.

  1. Name the operand with a 2-byte label:
  label dlivec=3:$55AC+1
     That gives dlivec equ *+1 above the jmp, and every writer becomes sta 
     dlivec / sta dlivec+1. The equ line now lists all 20 of them; it used to
     show only the writers of the first byte.
  2. Mark what's written, either by applying the suggestions in Problems
     (bomb-jack now gets 14 into this operand) or by hand:
     - $558D is a low-byte-only write: lo 3:$558E $5595 gives lda #<s3l5595. Of
       the 14 writes, 8 are like this.
     - The other 6 write both bytes: e.g. codeptr 3:$5139_5134 gives lda 
       #<s3l5140 / lda #>s3l5140, and also traces the handler.

  What changed to make the third step work:
  - Jump operands are code pointers. Writing into a jmp abs/jsr abs operand now
    counts as setting a code pointer, so pairs become codeptr (they were
    address). Messages say "the operand of jmp at $55AB".
  - Low-byte-only writes are detected. When only the low byte is written, the
    page is the one that lands on code: the writer's own page, or the operand's
    current high byte. For $558D that's $5595.
  - Overlay-aware targets. Bomb-jack loads many segments over $4000–$7FFF, and
    targets and names were looked up in the last one loaded. That's why your lo
    would have named s56l5595, and why messages said $55AC instead of dlivec.
    Detection and hi/lo targets now prefer the segment the instruction is in.

  The low-byte-only writes become lo directives, which only name the target;
  they don't trace it. Your handlers there are already traced through your code
  entries, which is what the suggestion requires anyway.

● Not hard. I'd estimate an afternoon, since the repeat machinery is already
  there for single-byte fills. Both assemblers accept a repeated multi-value
  line (:3 dta $01,$02 and :2 dta c'AB',$9B both assemble to the expected
  bytes).

  How it would work: where a data line starts, try pattern lengths 1–16 and see
  how far each repeats. Take the one that covers the most bytes, preferring the
  shortest pattern on ties, and emit :N dta … when it covers enough. It would
  stop at the same things a fill run stops at today (labels, comments, code,
  pointers, format changes), so byte picking, labels inside a run, and the
  round-trip guarantee keep working.

  The payoff is modest, though. I simulated it (patterns of 2–16 bytes, at least

  The "data lines" figures combine single-byte fills with patterns. Patterns

  mostly 2-byte alternations (bomb-jack's are likely graphics or sound data),
  some 8- and 16-byte rows, and boink's 9-byte records.

  One caveat: collapsing can hide structure. A table of 9-byte records reads
  better as rows than as :7 dta … once something is labeled inside it. So I'd
  add a "Repeat patterns up to N bytes" option next to Fill run minimum, set to
  0 to turn it off, with conservative thresholds. You could also stop it locally
  by marking a range as data or text.

● Repeated patterns are built and committed as e296c87. They're opt-in: set
  Project → Repeat patterns up to to, say, 16; 0 (the default) turns them off.

  A pattern is collapsed when it's up to that many bytes long, repeats at least
  3 times, and covers at least Fill run minimum bytes (32 by default). Runs stop
  at labels, comments, code, pointers and format changes, so labels inside a
  pattern, byte picking and comments keep working. The setting is saved with
  projects and in .dop exports. With patterns off, the output is exactly as
  before.

      :14 dta $00,$00,$00,$00,$00,$FF,$FF,$FF,$FF               ; 3171 (boink: 9-byte records)
      :4 dta $55,$55,$61,$61,$55,$61,$55,$61            ; 540D (bomber)
      :4 dta $DA,$13,$7E,$C0,$6F,$7E,$D5,$13,$7E,$C0,$6F,$7E            ; 5C98 (bomb-jack)

● No, xdis didn't detect it before; it does now. ldx #$2C / ldy #$E7 / lda #$07
  / jsr SETVBV at $2CAD installs a deferred VBI at $2CE7. The old register-pair
  check only made suggestions when the address already landed on traced code or
  a label, and $2CE7 is reachable only through this call.

  What changed: xdis now knows SETVBV's convention (Y = low byte, X = high byte,
  A = 6 for an immediate VBI or 7 for a deferred one). On Atari files, an
  immediate X and Y before jsr SETVBV is always suggested as a code pointer,
  labelled with the VBI kind:

  ▎ #$2C at $2CA7 and #$E7 at $2CA9 form $2CE7 (passed to SETVBV as the deferred
  ▎ VBI routine)

  Applying it adds codeptr $2CA8_2CAA, which gives:

      ldx #>l2CE7               ; 2CA7: A2 2C
      ldy #<l2CE7               ; 2CA9: A0 E7
      lda #$07          ; 2CAB: A9 07
      jsr SETVBV                ; 2CAD: 20 5C E4

  It also traces the VBI routine: in your project, traced instructions go from
  107 to 233. The suggestion dialog now previews the real instructions (ldx/ldy)
  rather than always lda.

  Testing: a new synthetic SETVBV round-trip case checks ldx #>l2010 / ldy 
  #<l2010 and the traced routine. All 34 cases reassemble byte-identical, the UI
  suite passes, and the README mentions the convention.

  About your file: abbayes-evilchurch.xdis.json is at the repo root, not in
  examples/. That means git doesn't ignore it, and the tests don't pick it up.
  I'd move it into examples/. Want me to move it, then commit the code changes
  (leaving the project file out)?

  Your local images make a good test set. Your Downloads folder has real .car

  ├──────┼────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤

  │ 13   │ bank fixed at $A000, a value   │ wee_a8_rc5.car                 │
  │      │ written to $D5xx picks the     │                                │
  │      │ bank at $8000                  │                                │
  ├──────┼────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │      │ Atarimax 1 MB (old): 128 × 8   │ scorch.car,                    │
  │ 42   │ KB at $A000, written address   │ Barbarian_oldMAX.car,          │
  │      │ $D5xx selects                  │ bubble-atarimax, …             │
  ├──────┼────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 54,  │ SIC! 128/512 KB                │ CosmicHero2Prologue.car, tony  │
  │ 56   │                                │ FREE.car                       │
  ├──────┼────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 71   │ 5200 Super Cart                │ wee.car                        │
  └──────┴────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────┘

  My recommendation: treat each bank as a segment. A banked cart is many blocks
  of ROM sharing one CPU address window, which is exactly the overlay problem
  xdis already handles for XEX files. Per-segment labels, segment-qualified
  directives (3:$A000), "prefer the instruction's own segment" lookups, and
  relocation all carry over.

  Phase 1: loading and output (about a day).
  - Loader: read .car files (CART header, cartridge type, checksum). For raw
    .bin/.rom images, offer the cart types that match the file size in the open
    dialog, the way atari800 does.
  - Cart type descriptors: a small table per scheme listing the window(s), bank
    size, fixed banks, the power-on bank, and how a bank is selected (by the
    value written, or by the address accessed). The families in your folder
    (standard, Williams, XEGS/switchable XEGS, Atarimax, SIC!) cover most real
    carts. MegaCart and the rest are table entries.
  - Output: opt h-, then the CART header as dta, then org $A000 (or $8000) per
    bank in file order. Since opt h- writes bytes sequentially, the output
    reassembles byte-identical under both xasm and MADS, and your files become
    round-trip tests.
  - Naming: labels and the UI would say "bank 5" instead of "segment 6", e.g.
    b5_lA123, and go-to would accept b5:A123.

  Phase 2: bank-aware tracing (another day or so). The real question is which
  bank is in the window when code jumps there:
  - Unambiguous cases: references within a bank stay in that bank (the same rule
    I just added for overlays), and references into a fixed bank are
    unambiguous.
  - Boot: start tracing from CARTCS/CARTAD in the power-on bank. Your new
    sys.dop names make this automatic.
  - Bank switches: track bank-select writes in straight-line code, reusing the
    register tracking from pointer detection. For example, lda #5 / sta $D500
    (XEGS) or sta $D505 (Atarimax/Williams) followed by jsr $8xxx means bank 5.
    The select instructions themselves could read as sta CARTBANK+5.
  - Unknown bank: where it can't be resolved, don't guess. A Problem would list
    "jsr into the bank window with an unknown bank at $A123", and a small new
    directive (bank $A123 5) would tell xdis that the operand at $A123 refers to
    bank 5. It could also be offered as a suggestion when a nearby select is
    found.
  - RAM trampolines: bank-switching code that's copied to RAM and run there can
    use the existing relocate.

  Caveats:
  - Huge carts: a 1 MB Atarimax cart gives 128 banks and a listing of a few
    hundred thousand lines. The virtual listing copes, but analysis will take
    seconds rather than milliseconds, so I'd make re-analysis smarter if it
    feels slow. The!Cart images (your 8.9 MB file) are probably out of scope.
  - 5200 carts: these use a different memory map and hardware, so they'd need
    their own symbol set. I'd treat them as a later add-on.

  Shall I start with Phase 1 for types 1, 2, 8, 13 and 42, using your files as
  round-trip tests?

● Phase 1 of cartridge support is committed as e56f01b; nothing is left
  uncommitted. All six of your .car files reassemble byte-identical.

  Loading:
  - Formats: .car files are detected by their CART header. Raw dumps get an
    "Atari cartridge (raw dump)" format with a cartridge-type list, with types
    matching the file size listed first.
  - Supported types (atari800 numbering): standard 2/4/8/16 KB, Williams (8,
    22, 76), XEGS and switchable XEGS (12–14, 23–25, 33–38, 67), Atarimax (41,
    42 with power-on bank $7F, 75), SIC! (54–56, 16 KB banks split into
    $8000/$A000 halves) and MegaCart (26–32, 64). Other types show as 8 KB banks
    at $A000, with a note in Problems.

  Banks:
  - One segment per bank, at its window address, named b0, b1, …. That name
    shows in the address column, inspector, map tooltips and Callers lists.
    Directives and go-to accept b5:$A123, and automatic labels are b5_lA123
    where banks overlap.
  - Power-on banks are analyzed last, so sys.dop names and directives without a
    bank refer to the boot configuration. The header vectors at $BFFA/$BFFE are
    traced automatically.
  - Project panel: a Banks table, with ⏻ marking the banks visible at power-on.
    The cartridge type can be changed there.

  Output: opt h-, the 16-byte .car header as dta, then a banner and org per
  bank. Both xasm and MADS write the bytes in order even though every bank
  restarts at the same address.

  go-to b2:8000, bank prefixes, boot tracing) pass on repeated runs.

  What Phase 2 would add: the low counts are what Phase 1 can't follow yet.
  Bank-switched carts reach most of their code through bank switches, and
  scorch.car boots by copying a loader to $0700 and running it there. A jump
  into a switched window currently resolves to the bank visible at power-on (or
  to the jumping instruction's own bank). Phase 2 would track the bank-select
  writes before such jumps, flag the jumps it can't resolve, and add the bank
  directive for those.

  Two other fixes along the way:
  - Startup crash: a broken string in my Banks-table edit stopped the app from
    loading at all. The UI tests caught it.
  - Stray COM caller: the "trace the first segment" fallback for headerless XEX
    files ran on cartridges. It no longer does.

  The README has a new Cartridges section. That's 16 local commits, none pushed
  yet.

❯ Should we have built-in bank-register labels that are automatically enabled   
  for the active cart type?                                                     

● Before recommending, I'll check whether the existing symbol sets already name
  anything at $D5xx:

  Searched for 1 pattern (ctrl+o to expand)

● Yes, I think so. Nothing labels $D5xx today, so a bank switch reads as a bare
  sta $D505 or lda $D500. The cartridge type already tells xdis exactly what
  those addresses do.

  How I'd do it:
  - Generated from the cartridge type, not a stored symbol set. The same
    descriptor table that lays out the banks would also describe the bank
    registers, and the analysis would add their labels automatically, the way it
    already adds the header vectors. Changing the cartridge type updates them,
    and nothing goes stale in saved projects. That also avoids the stale-copy
    problem we just had with sys.dop.
  - Visible and overridable. The labels would appear in the Directives panel as
    a read-only "Cartridge" set. Your own labels at those addresses still win,
    like any project label over a symbol set.
  - Names that show the bank where the scheme allows it. For address-select
    schemes (Williams, Atarimax), the bank is the offset:

  | Family                               | Labels                              |
  Example               |
  |--------------------------------------|-------------------------------------|
  -----------------------|
  | Atarimax 128 KB                      | CARTBANK=$D500+F, CARTOFF=$D510+F   |
  sta CARTBANK+5        |
  | Atarimax 1 MB                        | CARTBANK=$D500+7F, CARTOFF=$D580+7F |
  sta CARTBANK+12       |
  | Williams                             | CARTBANK=$D500+7, CARTOFF=$D508+7   |
  lda CARTBANK+3        |
  | XEGS, MegaCart, SIC! (value selects) | CARTBANK=$D500+FF                   |
  lda #5 / sta CARTBANK |
    For value-select schemes the bank is in the lda # before the store, which is
    what Phase 2's tracking would use. CARTBANK/CARTOFF aren't official Atari
    names (there aren't any), just neutral names taken from cart.txt's wording.

  Two details I'd adjust:
  - Decimal offsets: offsets above 9 are currently written in hex (CARTBANK+$C).
    For bank registers, decimal (+12) reads better, so I'd write offsets on
    these labels in decimal.
  - .dop export: the CLI doesn't know cartridges, so the export would write
    these as plain data lines rather than relying on xdis to regenerate them.

  How it fits with Phase 2: both come from the same register description in the
  descriptor (base address, address-select vs. value-select, disable range).
  Labels would come first as a small, standalone piece, and the bank tracking
  would reuse that table.

  Want me to go ahead with these names, or do you have names you already use for
  the bank registers?

  What you get per cartridge type:

  ┌─────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────┬──────────────────┐
  │      Types      │          Built-in labels          │     Reads as     │
  ├─────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │ Williams (8,    │ CARTBANK=$D500+(banks−1),         │ lda CARTBANK+3   │
  │ 22, 76)         │ CARTOFF=$D508+7                   │                  │
  ├─────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │ Atarimax 128 KB │ CARTBANK=$D500+F, CARTOFF=$D510+F │ sta CARTBANK+12  │
  │  (41)           │                                   │                  │
  ├─────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │ Atarimax 1 MB   │ CARTBANK=$D500+7F,                │ sta CARTBANK+100 │
  │ (42, 75)        │ CARTOFF=$D580+7F                  │                  │
  ├─────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │ XEGS, MegaCart, │ CARTBANK=$D500+FF                 │ lda #5 / sta     │
  │  SIC!           │                                   │ CARTBANK         │
  └─────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────┘

  How they behave:
  - Follow the type: they're generated from the cartridge type rather than
    stored in the project, so changing the type updates them.
  - Decimal offsets: these labels write offsets in decimal, so +12 is bank 12.
  - Read-only, lowest priority: they're listed under Directives as "Cartridge: …
    (built in)". Your own labels and symbol sets win; for example, data 
    bankreg=$D500+7 gives lda bankreg+3.
  - Export: .dop exports include them as plain data lines with a comment, since
    the CLI doesn't know cartridge types.

  Testing:
  - Your files: the XEGS and SIC! carts now show sta CARTBANK. Scorch and Red
    Max don't reach their bank-switch code until Phase 2.
  - Round trips: three synthetic cases cover sta CARTBANK+12 / sta CARTOFF
    (Atarimax), lda CARTBANK+3 (Williams), and the override. All 46 cases are
    byte-identical, and the UI suite passes.

  That's 17 local commits, none pushed yet.

● Phase 2 is committed as d05863c. And yes, you're on the right track with Red
  Max.

  Red Max: it's a loader. Bank 0's code is copied into RAM at $0600/$0670, which
  your two relocates handle correctly. From there, a table at $0600 (copied
  from $A000) drives a copy loop that moves nine pieces of the cartridge into
  RAM. That includes the RAM under the OS, because it writes $FE to PORTB first.
  Then it starts the game at $2400.

  So the rest is one relocate per table row. The Directives box now accepts a
  pasted block as one undoable change, so you can paste this:

  relocate b0:$A200+FFF $C000
  relocate b0:$B300+7FF $D800
  relocate b1:$A000+1FFF $E000
  relocate b2:$A000+1FFF $0A00
  relocate b3:$A000+1FFF $2A00
  relocate b4:$A000+1FFF $4A00
  relocate b5:$A000+1FFF $6A00
  relocate b6:$A000+1FFF $8A00
  relocate b7:$A000+15FF $AA00

  I tried this on your project: xdis then traces 1,977 instructions of the game
  from $2400, and the output reassembles byte-identical. Your existing codeptr 
  $6E5_6DF already starts tracing at $2400.

  One catch: since the game overwrites the OS area, sys.dop's OS entry points
  (CIOV, SIOV, SETVBV, WARMSV, COLDSV) end up labeling and tracing the game's
  own RAM there. For this project I'd turn sys.dop off.

  Phase 2: following bank switches while tracing. Each code path carries the
  current bank selection:
  - Address-select carts (Williams, Atarimax): any access to CARTBANK+n selects
    bank n.
  - Value-select carts (XEGS, MegaCart, SIC!): a store to CARTBANK selects the
    bank given by the value written, when it's known from a preceding lda #.
  - Effect: jumps, calls, branches and data accesses into the window then go to
    the selected bank, including code that switches its own window. Before any
    switch, the window holds the bank visible at power-on.
  - Unknown bank: when the bank can't be known (e.g. an indexed sta CARTBANK,x),
    the jump is listed in Problems. Clicking it asks for the bank and adds a
    new directive, bank b7:$A456 5. Target bank… in the context menu and
    inspector sets or overrides it for any instruction into a bank window.

  Results:
  - Your XEGS cart (wee_a8_rc5.car) goes from 2,063 to 3,659 traced
    instructions, now following switches into banks 3 and 6.
  - Red Max, scorch and SIC! are unchanged. They copy themselves to RAM, so
    relocate is the tool for them, as above.

  Testing:
  - Round trips: synthetic XEGS carts check a known switch (jsr b2_l8000), an
    unknown one listed in Problems, and a bank directive resolving it. All 49
    cases reassemble byte-identical.
  - UI suite: clicks the unknown-bank problem, chooses a bank, and pastes

● You can now dismiss suggestions, and the one at $BC87 doesn't appear in the
  first place anymore.

  Why it was suggested: your project declares colorcount2=$94+1, a 2-byte data
  range. The detection treated any 2-byte range as proof of a pointer, so #$FE /
  #$FF stored into it looked like $FFFE (IRQVEC). As you say, it's −2 in a
  16-bit counter.

  Fix 1: stricter evidence. A plain 2-byte data range no longer counts as proof
  of a pointer on its own: the value must also land on loaded code or a label.
  $FFFE isn't loaded in the Educational cart, so the suggestion is gone. Real
  pointer evidence still counts by itself: vector/address/codeptr directives,
  (P),y, (P,x) and jmp (P). The suggestions in your other projects still appear,
  and all 51 round-trip cases reassemble byte-identical.

  Fix 2: dismissing. Every suggestion in Problems now has a ×, and the
  suggestion dialogs have a Dismiss button. Either adds a dismiss $ADDR
  directive. It's undoable and listed under Directives, so deleting it brings
  the suggestion back. It works the same for relocation, pointer and hi/lo
  suggestions.

  Also fixed: a warning I introduced with the cartridge names in sys.dop.
  Bomb-jack loads $BFFE but not $BFFF, so CARTAD warned "pointer at $BFFE is in
  undefined memory". Problems from symbol-set directives are no longer reported,
  since those files describe the machine rather than your program. Bomb-jack
  now shows no problems.

  Testing: the UI tests dismiss a suggestion, check it disappears and that undo
  brings it back. A round-trip case checks a dismissed SETVBV pair isn't
  applied. Both pass, and the README covers dismissing.

  These changes, plus the Save binary button from before, aren't committed yet.
  Want me to commit them?

  right of the listing.

    operands, labels, comments, and the Access/Callers lists), so a search for
    an address like 9E16 finds it in comments too.
  - Options: Aa for match case and .* for regular expressions; a bad regex is
    flagged instead of erroring.

    Shift+Enter/Shift+F3 to the previous one, wrapping at either end. Ctrl+G /
    Ctrl+Shift+G work from the listing too. Esc closes it.
  - Live: matches update as you type, starting from the cursor. Matching rows
    are highlighted, the current one darker. Results also update after every
    edit.

  closing. They pass on repeated runs. The README key table and the ? help list
  the new keys.

● That's the hidden read: inc ZP,x with X = #$94 (the ldx #$94 / jsr 
  incword_at_x at $BC80). Let me see what values the other five stores write,
  and what happens around them:

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● You're right that colorcount2 is a misleading name. $94/$95 isn't store-only.
  It's read and incremented indirectly, which is why xdis's Access list only
  shows stores: attract does ldx #$94 / jsr incword_at_x, and incword_at_x does
  inc ZP,x / inc ZP+1,x. With X = $94, that's a read-modify-write of $94/$95
  that xdis can't attribute to the address.

  What it is: $92–$95 look like a 32-bit idle timer for an attract mode, i.e. a
  screen saver that cycles the colors when nobody is using the machine:
  - attract is called from the cart's idle polling loops: waitkey (via $B958),
    waitstartkeydown, waitstartkeyup and donesso.
  - Each call increments $92/$93. Only when that wraps to zero (every 65,536
    calls) does it increment $94/$95.
  - When $94/$95 reaches zero, it rotates the colors: it adds $33 to the
    playfield and player color shadows and $55 to the background shadow, writes
    them to COLPF1/COLPF2/COLPMn/COLBK, and reloads $94/$95 with $FFFE. From
    then on the colors change every 2 wraps of the low word.

  So $94/$95 is the high word, counting up toward zero, and the stores you saw
  set the delay:

  ┌───────────────────────────────┬───────────────────┬────────────────────┐
  │                               │                   │ Wraps of $92/$93   │
  │             Where             │       Value       │ until the colors   │
  │                               │                   │       change       │
  ├───────────────────────────────┼───────────────────┼────────────────────┤
  │ enableserial ($B8D9),         │ $FEFE (lda #$FE   │                    │
  │ readdone ($B951), wrong       │ stored into both  │ 258                │
  │ ($B973)                       │ bytes)            │                    │
  ├───────────────────────────────┼───────────────────┼────────────────────┤
  │ correct ($B900), checksso     │                   │                    │
  │ ($B930) when a console key is │ $FBFB             │ 1,029              │
  │  down                         │                   │                    │
  ├───────────────────────────────┼───────────────────┼────────────────────┤
  │ inside attract ($BC87), once  │ $FFFE             │ 2                  │
  │ it's running                  │                   │                    │
  └───────────────────────────────┴───────────────────┴────────────────────┘

  The $FBFB paths and the wrong path also call restorecolors, which puts the
  original colors back. So user activity cancels any attract mode in progress
  and restarts the countdown: a correct answer or a console key gives a longer
  grace period than the others.

  Suggested names, either:
  data idletimer=$92+3          ; 32-bit attract-mode countdown
  or, to keep the two halves separate:
  data idletimer_lo=$92+1
  data idletimer_hi=$94+1
  In both cases colorcount1 at $92 is part of the same counter, so it was
  probably mislabeled too.

  Not tracking accesses made through a routine called with an address in X is a
  general gap in xdis. A future suggestion could flag ldx #$94 / jsr into a
  routine that uses zp,x, so these accesses show up in Access lists. Want me to
  look into that?

● Both are done.

  Viewing symbol sets: every symbol set in the Directives panel (built-in or
  imported) now has a view button. It opens a searchable table of the set's
  labels, taken from the .dop text so the original descriptions and section
  headings stay (e.g. "VECTOR TABLE", "JUMP VECTOR TABLE"):
  - Columns: name, address or range, kind (data/vector/code), and the
    description from the file.
  - Filter: by name, address or description; e.g. "vector" narrows sys.dop's 291
    labels to 34.
  - Used here: labels the current program actually uses are marked ●, and Only 
    used here shows just those (41 in your Galaxian project).
  - Go to: clicking a row closes the viewer and jumps to that address (or its
    equ line).

  Consistent naming: the inspector's Callers and Accessed-by lists now name
  segments exactly like the listing's comments: b0:B8BD for cartridge banks,
  with no prefix for relocated code at an unambiguous address. That was the only
  place using raw segment numbers.

  I added UI tests for the viewer (full list, descriptions, filter, only-used,
  clicking a row) and for the bank names in the inspector. They pass on repeated
  runs.

● Good use case: Red Max is exactly where you'd want to switch off sys.dop's
  CIOV, SIOV and friends rather than the whole set. Here's the design:
  - Effect: a disabled label is dropped from that set completely, so its label
    and any effect on tracing go away (e.g. code CIOV=$E456 no longer traces).
    The rest of the set stays on.
  - Viewer: each row in the symbol-set viewer gets a checkbox, plus Disable 
    shown / Enable shown buttons for the current filter (e.g. filter $E4 to
    switch off the OS jump table in one go). Every change is one undoable step,
    and the viewer stays open.
  - Directives panel: shows how many labels are off next to each set's name.
  - Saving: the list is saved in the project. .dop exports record it as an ;xdis
    off sys.dop CIOV SIOV … line, which the CLI ignores and xdis restores on
    import.

● Individual labels in a symbol set can now be switched on and off from the
  set's viewer.

  - Per label: each row has a checkbox. Unticking it removes that label
    completely (its name and any effect on tracing), and it's shown struck out.
    The rest of the set keeps working. Each change is one undoable step.
  - In bulk: Disable shown / Enable shown apply to whatever the filter shows.
    For example, $e4 in sys.dop selects the 22 OS vectors and jump-table entries
    at $E4xx (CIOV, SIOV, SETVBV, …), which is what you'd switch off for Red

  the vectors at $0200 (USERV, BRKV, IRQ1V, BYTEV, …), zero page $B0–$FF, OS
  variables $0236–$02FF, VDU variables $0300–$037F, sideways ROM header at
  $8000
  Entries: 385
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Set: bbchw.dop
  Contents: Model B hardware in SHEILA ($FE00–$FEFF): CRTC, ACIA, serial and
  video ULAs, romsel, system and user VIAs, FDC, Econet, ADC, Tube; plus the
  FRED and JIM pages
  Entries: 70
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  Set: bbcmosbuf.dop
  Contents: MOS buffers and workspace in $0380–$0E00 (cassette, keyboard buffer,

  sound, soft keys and characters, NMI area). Opt-in, because games often reuse
   this RAM
  Entries: 125

  Where the names come from:
  - OS entry points and vectors: Acorn's official names from the Advanced User
    Guide, with descriptions from py8dis.
  - Hardware registers: py8dis (MIT license), e.g. system_via_ier. The generator
    runs py8dis's own hardware() function for the Model B, so its
    machine-specific choices are followed exactly. The many optional FRED add-on
    devices (MIDI, SID, Teletext…) are left out.
  - MOS workspace: the chapter on memory addresses in Toby Nelson's MOS 1.20
    reassembly, the page you suggested. I used only direct definitions, not his
    many context-specific aliases, and left out his comments because they wrap
    mid-sentence in the source. That site states no license, unlike py8dis.
    Names are close to bare facts, and the generator credits him in each file
    header, but check you're comfortable with it before publishing.

  The names keep their sources' styles: uppercase for Acorn's official names,
  snake_case from py8dis, camelCase from the MOS reassembly. I didn't rename
  anything, so each name can be traced back to where it came from.

  To rebuild after the sources change, run tools/harvest-bbc.py; it downloads
  them into .cache/. Then run tools/embed-symbols.py.

● I looked at l865C and its two call sites. You're mostly right, with one twist
  that matters for how we model it.

  l865C   pla / sta $B0 / pla / sta $B1     ; pop the return address (= jsr+2)
          ldy #0
  l8664   inc $B0 / bne / inc $B1          ; step to the next byte
          lda ($B0),y
          bmi l8674                        ; stop at the first byte with bit 7 
  set
          jsr OSASCI                       ; print it
          jmp l8664
  l8674   jmp ($B0)                        ; continue AT that byte

  It never adjusts the stack and returns. It pops the return address, prints
  bytes until it finds one ≥ $80, then jmps to that byte. The terminator isn't 
  data. It's the first opcode of the code that follows. At $8232, "Econet
  Station " is followed by $A0 $14 = ldy #$14, and that's where execution
  resumes. (This is the Acorn NFS 3.60 ROM paged in at $8000, and the trick is a
  common Acorn one.)

  Today the tracer gets both call sites wrong:
  - $8208: it keeps decoding after the jsr as code. That produces ora l464E and
    a bogus l464E label from the text.
  - $8232: your text $8237+F directive includes the $A0, so ldy #$14 / lda 
    ($9C),y … is never traced as code.

  Recommendation: an inline directive on the routine

  The convention belongs to the routine, so it should be declared once rather
  than marked at every call site:

  inline l865C=$865C   ;xdis inline text, until bit7, resume at terminator

  The tracer would then do this at every jsr to that routine:
  1. Scan from jsr+3 to the end of the inline data.
  2. Render that range as text or bytes. This is a local kind, so you don't need
     a text directive per call and nothing gets dropped into the .dop.
  3. Continue tracing at the resume point and add it as a code entry. The
     Callers: comment shows it's reached from the jsr.

  I'd support a few presets, because most inline-argument routines use one of
  them:

  ┌──────────┬─────────────────────┬─────────────────────┬──────────────────┐
  │  Preset  │      Data ends      │     Resumes at      │     Seen in      │
  ├──────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │ bit7     │ first byte ≥ $80    │ the terminator      │ Acorn NFS/DFS    │
  │          │                     │ (this case)         │                  │
  ├──────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │ bit7incl │ byte with bit 7 set │ after it            │ many print       │
  │          │  (last char)        │                     │ routines         │
  ├──────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │ zero     │ $00                 │ after it            │ PRIMM on         │
  │          │                     │                     │ Apple/C64        │
  ├──────────┼─────────────────────┼─────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │ bytes N  │ fixed N bytes       │ after them          │ jsr setptr /     │
  │          │                     │                     │ .word arg        │
  └──────────┴─────────────────────┴─────────────────────┴──────────────────┘

  Output still reassembles byte-identically, because it's only dta versus code.

  Detection

  The prologue pla / sta zp / pla / sta zp+1 is a strong signature that a
  routine reads its own return address. The suggestion engine could flag it like
  the SETVBV and pointer-pair detections ("l865C pulls its return address —
  inline arguments?"). For the common shapes, it can also guess the preset:
  - lda (zp),y followed by bmi or beq gives the terminator.
  - jmp (zp) without a following inc means "resume at terminator".
  - pha / pha / rts means "resume after".

  You'd review the guess and accept it, or dismiss it.

  comment gave '\t'.repeat(-1), which would also have broken Save .asm for such
  projects. I changed it to Math.max(1, …), which leaves output for shorter
  labels unchanged. I haven't re-run the tests since this fix.

  Shall I implement the inline directive with these presets and the detection?
  I'd also add a round-trip case for l865C, and commit the tab fix along with it
  or on its own, whichever you prefer.

      218  `label dlivec=3:$55AC+1`, to get `dlivec equ *+1` and `sta dli
           vec` /
      219  `sta dlivec+1`.
      220  
      221 +### Inline data after calls                                   
      222 +                                                              
      223 +Some routines take their arguments from the bytes after the `j
          +sr`. They pull                                                
      224 +the return address off the stack, read through it, and continu
          +e past the data.                                              
      225 +An `inline` directive on the routine tells the tracer how to f
          +ind the end of                                                
      226 +the data at every call:                                       
      227 +                                                              
      228 +    inline $865C bit7       ; text up to a byte with bit 7 set
          +, which is the next instruction                               
      229 +    inline $865C bit7last   ; text whose last byte has bit 7 s
          +et; continues after it                                        
      230 +    inline $865C zero       ; text ending in a zero byte; cont
          +inues after it                                                
      231 +    inline $865C 2          ; a fixed number of bytes (1-255) 
      232 +                                                              
      233 +The data after each call becomes `dta`, and tracing continues 
          +where the routine

      jsr l865C           ; 8208
      dta $0D,c'NFS 3.60',$0D
  l8215 ...               ; terminator is the next instruction (ldy l00A8)
      jsr l865C           ; 8232
      dta c'Econet Station '
  l8244                   ; Callers: l8232
      ldy #$14            ; the $A0 terminator, now traced as code
      ...
      jsr l865C           ; 8252: this call was hidden inside your text $8252 
  range
      dta c' No Clock'

  The bogus ora l464E and its l464E label after $8208 are gone.

  Delete these three directives in your project: text $8235+1, text $8237+F and
  text $8252+11. They cover the terminator bytes, so they stop tracing at the
  resume points. The unneeded-directive scan won't flag them, because they
  change the result. code $822F and code $8232 are probably unneeded now, and
  the scan will tell you.

  How it works:
  - Directive: inline [name=][seg:]$ROUTINE MODE. The modes are:
    - bit7: data runs up to a byte with bit 7 set, and that byte is the next
      instruction;
    - bit7last: the last data byte has bit 7 set, and execution continues after
      it;
    - zero: data ends in a zero byte, and execution continues after it;
    - a decimal byte count from 1 to 255.

    It's stored as a ;xdis inline … line, and I checked that it survives a .dop
    export and re-import.
  - Tracer: at each jsr to that routine it marks the inline bytes as text (or as
    plain bytes for a count). Tracing then continues where the routine returns,
    and the resume point shows the jsr as its caller. If no end turns up within
    256 bytes, or the data runs into unloaded memory, a problem is reported.
  - Detection: it looks for routines called by jsr that start with pla / sta P /
    pla / sta P+1 and then read lda (P),y. A bmi/bpl after the read means bit 7
    ends the text and beq/bne means zero. A jmp (P) means execution resumes at
    the terminator. None of your other six example projects gets a suggestion.
  - UI:
    - Inline data after calls… is in the right-click menu on a jsr or on the
      routine's first instruction.
    - The dialog has a choice for each mode, a box for a byte count, a preview
      of the directive, and None to remove an existing one.
    - Suggestions open the same dialog with Dismiss.
    - Apply all for pointer suggestions leaves inline suggestions alone.
  - Docs: the README has a new "Inline data after calls" section.

  Also fixed: the lineText crash I mentioned earlier (js/core.js). A label of 32
  or more characters with a comment threw an error, which also broke Save .asm.

❯ Can you propose other methods to automate data/code classification?           

● Here are the methods I'd consider, best value for effort first. Each would
  follow the pattern we already use: detect it, put it in Problems as a
  suggestion, and let you review it, apply it or dismiss it.

  1. Jump tables and dispatch idioms

  These are probably the biggest source of untraced code. Common shapes:
  - RTS trick: lda tbl+1,x / pha / lda tbl,x / pha / rts. The table holds each
    target address minus 1.
  - Split tables: lda lo,x / sta P / lda hi,x / sta P+1 / jmp (P). The low and
    high bytes sit in two parallel tables.
  - Word tables: lda tbl,x / sta P / lda tbl+1,x / sta P+1 / jmp (P).

  We can find the table length from a bounds check (cpx #N / bcs). Failing that,
  we stop when an entry no longer points at plausible code. The RTS trick needs
  a small new pointer form with a −1 offset, such as codeptr $9000+F -1. pha / 
  pha / rts with immediates is the same thing for a single target.

  2. Import an execution trace from an emulator

  This is the most reliable evidence: an address that ran is code, whatever the
  static analysis says. You'd play the game in an emulator, export the executed
  addresses, and xdis would turn them into code entry points, plus data for
  addresses that were only read. For example, MAME's trace command writes one
  line per executed instruction, and several emulators have similar trace or
  profiler output. Parsing a list of program-counter values is simple, and it
  catches every indirect jump, jump table and interrupt handler that was
  reached. The cost is that you have to play through the parts you want covered.

  3. Score untraced gaps

  Each untraced region would get a "looks like code" score from a decode of it:
  - Points for: valid documented opcodes; branches that land on instruction
    boundaries inside the region; ending in rts/jmp; known labels and hardware
    registers as operands; common idioms like lda/sta pairs; starting right
    after an rts or jmp.
  - Points against: illegal opcodes, brk, and branches into the middle of an
    instruction.

  High scores become suggestions ("$4A10–$4A6F looks like an uncalled routine"),
  and the memory map could shade likely code. This is cheap and works on any
  platform. It needs tuning on your example projects to keep false positives
  down.

  4. Data typing for regions already known to be data

  - Text: runs of printable ASCII, ATASCII or PETSCII, Atari screen codes, and
    strings ending in a byte with bit 7 set or a zero.
  - Pointer tables: consecutive words that all point at code or labels.
  - Split lo/hi tables: two tables of equal length that the same routine reads
    with the same index.
  - Table sizes: taken from how they're accessed (lda tbl,x with cpx #N), so a
    data range gets the right length and a name.

  5. Platform structures

  - Atari display lists: found through SDLSTL/DLISTL writes, which we already
    detect as pointers. We'd parse the display-list instructions, so LMS
    operands become screen-memory pointers and JVB closes the loop.
  - Fonts and graphics: the CHBASE/PMBASE pages we already resolve get marked as
    1 KB font data or player/missile graphics.
  - C64: sprite pointers and charset bases from VIC register writes.
  - BBC: vectors written at run time (IRQ1V, EVNTV, …), found from their sta
    pairs, become code pointers.

  6. More constant tracking in the tracer

  The tracer already follows register values for bank switching. Extending that
  to zero-page pointers would resolve jmp (P) when P was set from immediates on
  the same path. Without it, that only shows up as a pointer suggestion. With
  it, the targets are traced directly and no directive is needed.

  7. Consistency checks

  These flag places where a classification is probably wrong:
  - traced code that runs into brk or into text;
  - two traces that disagree about where an instruction starts;
  - a branch into the middle of an instruction (other than the bit skip trick we
    already handle);
  - data that code reads with a jmp.

  8. Routine signatures

  Known routines (decompressors, multiply/divide, cc65 runtime helpers, common
  print routines like l865C) would be matched by their byte patterns. They'd get
  names automatically, and conventions like inline too.

  Recommendation

  I'd start with 1 (jump tables) and 3 (gap scoring). Together they should cover
  most of what's still untraced in projects like Bomb Jack and Ransack, and
  they reuse the suggestion machinery. 2 (trace import) is the best addition
  after that if you're happy to export traces from an emulator. Which ones would
  you like me to take on?

● I found that graphics bytes were being misclassified as valid code because the
  evidence check relied too heavily on zero-page labels. I'll replace it with a
  statistical likelihood score based on traced vs. untraced opcode frequency,
  stop treating rti as a block terminator, restrict label evidence to absolute
  operands, and tighten the evaluation so blocks landing on project-classified
  data count as false positives.
