● All three are implemented: jump tables (1), finding untraced code (3) and
  machine structures (5). All 71 round-trip cases and 152 UI checks pass; none
  of it is committed yet.

  1. Jump tables
  - What it finds: lda hi,x / pha / lda lo,x / pha / rts and lda lo,x / sta P / 
    lda hi,x / sta P+1 / jmp (P), as either a word table or two split tables.
    The size comes from a cpx #N / bcs check if there is one, otherwise from how
    many entries in a row point at code.
  - New pointer form: a trailing rts, as in codeptr $A642_A62B+16 rts, means
    each entry is the address minus 1. It renders as dta <[lA558-1]. The
    brackets are needed because both xasm and MADS read >l-1 as (>l)-1.
  - Result: in Altirra BASIC it finds the statement and function tables (23 and
    82 entries). Applying them takes traced instructions from 584 to 2,457.
  - Not covered: tables with only a low byte and a fixed high byte (lda #$9C / 
    pha / lda tbl,y / pha / rts), and Acorn's name-plus-address command tables.
    Both appear in the NFS/DFS code in Ransack; I can add them if you want.

  3. Code nothing traces into
  - How it decides: untraced bytes are decoded from every address. A block
    counts as code if:
    - it ends in rts, rti or jmp;
    - its branches and calls land on its own instructions, on traced code, on a
      label, or on another block that passes the same test;
    - its opcodes score as typical 6502 code. The scoring uses a profile I built
      from six programs (Atari and BBC games and cartridges), mixed with the
      program's own traced code.
  - How I checked it: I removed the code and data directives from each example
    project and applied the suggestions over several rounds. Recall is 91% for
    Galaxian, 78% for Bomb Jack and 28% for Ransack. Nothing it traced landed on
    bytes a project marks as data.
  - What else it found: real routines nobody had traced yet, such as Red Max's
    loader, uncalled sound code in abbayes, and Bomb Jack's DLIs and
    decompressor.
  - Bulk apply: Problems has an Apply all N code suggestions button, because
    Bomb Jack gets around 175.

  5. Machine structures
  - Atari: display lists from SDLSTL/DLISTL, with their LMS and jump operands as
    addresses, following JVB chains. Character sets from CHBAS/CHBASE. In the
    examples this finds Galaxian's 240-line display list, and three display
    lists and three fonts in Bomb Jack.
  - C64: character sets from $D018, using the VIC bank from $DD00, and sprite
    data from the sprite pointers.
  - BBC: OSWORD (by call number), OSFILE and OSGBPB blocks, and OSCLI/OSFIND
    strings, all addressed by X/Y. These are tested only on synthetic code,
    because Ransack's own calls don't load X/Y from immediates.
  - How it's applied: each structure is one suggestion that adds all of its
    directives.

  Changes you'll notice:
  - Machine detection: the machine now comes from the file type or the symbol
    sets in use. Before this, raw dumps like Ransack were treated as Atari, so
    the pointer detector checked Atari registers such as PMBASE there.
  - Slower analysis: it now takes 63 ms per edit on Bomb Jack, up from 16 ms,
    and 36 ms on Ransack, up from 8 ms. Most of the cost is decoding Bomb Jack's
    ~90 KB of untraced code, and it drops as code gets traced. The
    unneeded-directive scan skips all the detectors.

  UI: jump tables, untraced code and structures all open a review dialog. It

● Yes. l9FB8, l9FA3 and l9FAE are now all detected as inline routines in
  Ransack. Nothing is committed yet.

  What l9FB8 does: it's the DFS routine that raises a disk error. After each jsr
  there's an error number, then text, then either:
  - a byte with bit 7 set, where execution continues as code; or
  - a $00, after which it raises the error and doesn't return.

  l9FA3 and l9FAE are wrappers. They call l9FB8 with "Disk " or "Bad ", and the
  byte ending that text is a bcc l9FCF instruction. That jumps back into the
  error routine at l9FCF, which then reads the text after the wrapper's own jsr.

  The detector missed l9FB8 for two reasons. It pulls its return address after
  some other setup code rather than first thing, and there's a sta between
  reading each byte and testing it.

  Changes:
  - Two new inline options:
    - lead N: the first N bytes are data whatever their value. Here that's the
      error number, which can be ≥ $80, like $C7.
    - brk: a $00 ends the text and the routine doesn't return.

    So l9FB8 gets inline $9FB8 bit7 lead 1 brk.
  - Detection is more general:
    - A routine counts if it's the target of a real jsr and pulls its return
      address before doing anything else with the stack.
    - Instructions that don't change the flags may sit between the read and its
      test.
    - Reads before the tested one become lead.
    - A test for both bit 7 and zero means brk.
  - Wrappers: a routine whose jsr to an inline routine continues into a jump to
    an inline entry gets that entry's convention.
  - UI and docs: the inline dialog has a field for the lead bytes and a checkbox
    for brk, and the README is updated.

  Ransack, applying the suggestions in rounds:

● I added a Remove N directives with no effect button to the Directives panel.
  It isn't committed yet.

  - What it removes: the directives the background check already tags no effect.
    Those are code and data directives without a name, for bytes that tracing
    reaches anyway.
  - When it appears: once the check has finished and there's at least one to
    remove. Removing them is one step, so Ctrl+Z brings them back.
  - What stays: name only and format only directives, because they still change
    the output (a label name, or how bytes are shown as text, words or
    pointers).

  The existing check decides directives one at a time, counting the ones it has
  already ruled out, so removing only the no effect ones isn't guaranteed to
  keep the code the same. Before removing, the button re-analyses without them
  and checks the traced code is identical. If it isn't, it rechecks just those
  directives one by one and removes only the ones that are safe. In the example
  projects that fallback was never needed: Ransack has 8 to remove, the others
  none.

  Tests: all 73 round-trip cases and 156 UI checks pass. The four new UI checks
  cover:
  - the button appearing;
  - the right number of directives being removed;
  - the traced code staying the same;
  - undo.

  The README describes the button.

● No: $AEA2 itself should never lead to $AEAE, but the untraced-code finder
  should have suggested $AEAE, and it now does. That needed a fix in the finder,
  which isn't committed yet.

  Why $AEA2 doesn't lead there: jsr l9FA3 is followed by $C8,'changed',$00.
  Under the bit7 lead 1 brk convention, a $00 ends the text and raises a
  "changed" error, so execution never returns after that call. The tracer is
  right to stop, and the bytes at $AEAE only follow the error message.

  Why it wasn't suggested: $AEAE is real code that nothing traced reaches. The
  finder decoded it as 44 good-looking instructions, then hit jsr l9FB8 at $AF0A
  and decoded the inline text "Too many open" as instructions. That produced a
  bad opcode, so the whole block was rejected. The tracer knew about inline
  routines; the finder didn't.

  Fix (in js/core.js): at a jsr to an inline routine, the finder now skips the
  data the same way the tracer does. If the data ends without a return (brk),
  the block ends there as it would at an rts. If a branch earlier in the block
  jumps past that point, decoding continues after the data instead.

  Result on ransack-main.xdis (2).json: the finder now suggests 7 blocks.
  $AEAE-$AF19 is one of them; four others had been rejected the same way.
  Applying $AEAE gives:

      jsr l9FA3
      dta $C8,c'changed',$00
  lAEAE
      and #$C0
      bne lAEB8
      jsr lA327
      jmp lAE10

  Tests: all 75 round-trip cases and 156 UI checks pass, and the finder's
  evaluation on the example projects is unchanged. The new round-trip case is an
  uncalled routine that branches around an error call with inline data.

● $9A46 wasn't suggested because of a rule in the untraced-code finder that was
  too strict. It's fixed now, but not committed yet.

  Why it was missed: the routine at $9A46 decodes fine, but its beq at $9A72
  goes to $9A14. That address isn't traced code, so the finder checks it as a
  block of its own. $9A14 is just pla / tax / jmp $99A4, the tail end of another
  untraced routine that starts at $99F2. I required a branch target to meet the
  same bar as a suggestion (at least 4 instructions and a minimum score), so
  this 3-instruction tail failed. That sank $9A46, and with it $99F2.

  Fix: a branch or call target now only has to decode as valid instructions and
  score at least zero. It no longer needs evidence of its own, because the block
  that branches to it supplies that. Suggestions themselves still need the full
  evidence.

  Checking that against the example projects turned up an older problem. When
  text sits right before a routine, decoding can start in the text and run into
  the code. In Ransack, "…HERE" before $1C9D was included this way. When the
  finder finds a block, it now tries later starting points within the first 32
  bytes that end in the same place, and keeps the best-scoring one.

    $99F2-$9A2A and $9A46-$9A78.

  - No suggestion lands on bytes a project marks as data.

  block whose branch goes to a short tail, and a routine with text just before
  it. Both fail without the fix.

● I added the section keys:

  ┌───────┬─────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Key  │            Jumps to             │
  ├───────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │ ] / [ │ next / previous section of code │
  ├───────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │ } / { │ next / previous section of data │
  └───────┴─────────────────────────────────┘

  A section is a run of instructions, or of data lines (bytes, text, pointers).
  Labels, comments and equates don't break a run. Segment and org lines do, so
  code that continues in the next segment counts as a new section. Going
  backward first goes to the start of the current section, like vim's [[, and
  Esc returns from a jump. The keys are in the ? help and the README.

  The UI suite now passes 163 checks, including seven new ones for forward and
  backward jumps, starting inside a section, and Esc. Nothing is committed yet.

● $8854 wasn't suggested because of two weaknesses in the untraced-code finder.
  Both are fixed, but not committed yet. With the fixes, the finder suggests
  $8853-$88D0.

  The routine starts one byte earlier than you expected, at the pha at $8853.
  Its early exit, beq $88CD, lands on the matching pla / ldy $BC / rts.

  1. An unknown entry point at the end of a call chain. The finder rejects a
  block when a call target can't be shown to be code. Here the calls run $8854 →
  $85F7 → $9630 → $9B6E → $9C2F → $9C8E → $9ECA → jsr $0406. $0406 is the BBC's
  Tube entry point, and its code isn't in this memory dump. Traced code already
  calls it (jsr l0406 at $9A31), but the finder didn't count that. That one
  address rejected the whole chain.

  Fix: a target that traced code already calls or jumps to now counts as known,
  even if its code isn't in the image.

  2. Conditional branches used as jumps. $85F7 also calls $8510, a copy loop
  that exits through a beq. Its closing bne is followed by text ("SP.", "E."),
  so decoding past it hit an illegal opcode and the block was rejected.

  Fix: when the bytes after a conditional branch don't decode, the block may end
  at that branch, as long as no earlier branch jumps past it.

● Yes. I'll make it low effort: the tracer only looks at the single instruction
  just before a branch.

  ┌─────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │     Before      │              Branch that's always taken               │
  ├─────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ lda/ldx/ldy     │ bne/beq (from whether the value is zero), bpl/bmi     │
  │ #imm            │ (from bit 7)                                          │
  ├─────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ clc / sec       │ bcc / bcs                                             │
  ├─────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ clv             │ bvc                                                   │
  └─────────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  When the branch is always taken, the tracer follows only the target and
  doesn't decode the bytes after it, which are often data.

  There's one catch. If something else jumps straight to that branch
  instruction, the flags there are unknown, so the code after the branch could
  still run. The tracer remembers each branch it treated as forced. When another
  path arrives at it by a jump, it traces what comes after the branch after
  all.

  it are no longer traced from that path, because they're often data. Nothing is
  committed yet.

  What counts as forced: only the single instruction just before the branch is
  checked, as you asked.

  ┌───────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   Instruction     │             Branch that's always taken              │
  │      before       │                                                     │
  ├───────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ lda/ldx/ldy #imm  │ bne if the value isn't zero, beq if it is; bpl/bmi  │
  │                   │ by bit 7                                            │
  ├───────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ clc / sec         │ bcc / bcs                                           │
  ├───────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ clv               │ bvc                                                 │
  └───────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  If something else jumps straight to the branch instruction, the flags there
  are unknown. The tracer remembers each branch it treated as forced, and traces
  what comes after it when another path arrives by a jump.

❯ Do you know why the disassembly redraws slower when click-dragging the        
  scrollbar than when click-dragging the memory map?                            

  Searched for 3 patterns, ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● Yes. From the code, it comes down to when each path redraws relative to when
  the browser repaints.

  Dragging the memory map: the pointermove handler sets scrollTop and calls
  draw() straight away, in the same event (js/app.js:2664). The new scroll
  position and the new rows reach the screen together.

  Dragging the scrollbar: the browser scrolls the listing first, and modern
  browsers do that off the main thread. The rows already in the page get moved
  to the new position before any of our code runs. Only then does a scroll event
  arrive, and that handler just asks for a redraw on a later frame with
  requestAnimationFrame(draw) (js/app.js:2571). So each step of the drag shows
  at least one frame of the old rows at the new position. The listing is
  virtual: draw() only builds the visible lines plus 4 above and 4 below. Any
  jump bigger than a few lines therefore scrolls into empty space, then fills in
  a frame later, which reads as slow and flickery.

  There's also a small inefficiency: every scroll event queues its own draw.
  When several arrive in one frame, the listing gets rebuilt several times.

  I can't make the scrollbar redraw exactly like the map does without replacing
  the native scrollbar with a custom one. These would close most of the gap:

  1. Draw right away in the scroll handler instead of on the next frame, which
     removes the extra frame of lag.
  2. Queue at most one draw per frame, so the listing isn't rebuilt several
     times over.
  3. Draw a full screen above and below instead of 4 lines. Moderate jumps then
     land on rows that already exist, and only very fast drags would briefly
     show blank space. That costs roughly three times as many rows per draw.
     They're plain HTML strings, so that should be fine.

  Want me to make those changes?

● I've made the scrolling changes, but not quite as proposed, and they're not
  committed yet.

  What changed:
  - A full screen of rows above and below the visible area, instead of 4 lines.
    A scroll step that stays within those rows is already on screen correctly.
  - Redraw only near the edge. Each scroll just moves the box on the memory map.
    The rows are rebuilt only when the visible area gets within half a screen
    of the drawn rows' edge.
  - At most one redraw per burst of scroll events, run straight after the event
    with a zero-delay timer, not on the next animation frame.
  - overflow-anchor: none on the listing, which suits a list whose rows get
    replaced while scrolling.

  What I dropped: redrawing inside the scroll event itself. With that version,
  the UI tests occasionally failed because Chrome closed the open symbol viewer
  dialog: 2–3 runs in 15. The committed code never did: 0 in 15. I couldn't find
  the root cause. Instrumentation showed the browser closing the dialog itself,
  with no cancel, no submit and no app code involved. Waiting for the next
  animation frame instead also turned out unreliable in a hidden frame. The
  zero-delay timer passed all 165 UI checks in 15 out of 15 runs.

  The trade-off: the redraw runs just after the scroll event rather than inside
  it. That's usually before the next paint, but not guaranteed. So a fast
  scrollbar drag past the drawn rows may still show a frame of blank rows,
  though much less often than before. I could only check this in headless
  Chrome, which doesn't show what you see when dragging, so try it in your
  browser.

  Tests: all 165 UI checks pass, including two new ones. A small scroll keeps
  the rows already drawn, and a long jump redraws the visible lines. I also made
  two existing viewer checks report details when they fail. The round-trip
  tests don't touch this code.

  Want me to commit js/app.js, css/xdis.css and test/ui-test.html, leaving out
  your symbol-set edits?

● The batching is in the scroll listener in bind(), at js/app.js:2596:

  let scrollPending = false;
  lst.addEventListener('scroll', () => {
      if (scrollPending) return;
      scrollPending = true;
      setTimeout(() => { scrollPending = false; scrolled(); }, 0);
  }, { passive: true });

  The first scroll event sets scrollPending and schedules one zero-delay timer.
  Any further scroll events before that timer runs return straight away. When
  the timer fires, it clears the flag and calls scrolled() once, which reads the
  current scrollTop.

  scrolled() is at js/app.js:341. It only rebuilds the rows (via draw()) when
  the visible lines get within half a screen of the drawn rows' edge. Otherwise
  it just moves the box on the memory map.

  The "burst" is in practice a small one. Browsers send at most one scroll event
  per frame, so while you drag the scrollbar this usually batches just one
  event. It only merges several when more arrive before the timer gets to run,
  for example when the main thread is busy. So it mainly protects against
  redundant redraws rather than doing much batching during a normal drag.

● Yes. The listing's content will stop scrolling natively, and a separate narrow
  element showing only its scrollbar will drive it:

  - #listing becomes overflow-y: hidden. The browser can't scroll it on its own,
    so nothing on screen moves until our code redraws. It's still a scroll
    container, so the existing code that sets scrollTop keeps working.
  - A new scrollbar element next to it scrolls natively and contains only a
    spacer as tall as the listing. Its scroll event sets the listing's scrollTop
    and redraws. The rows and their position then change together, as with the
    memory-map drag.
  - The mouse wheel and touch drags over the listing are handled by our code.
  - Any other change to the listing's position (cursor keys, go to, find)
    updates the scrollbar to match.

● All 88 pass, and the new case fails without the fix. A UI run:

  Ran 1 shell command (ctrl+o to expand)

● $E31D wasn't marked as a BRK error because its zero byte was already claimed
  as the end of the error before it. It's fixed, but not committed yet.

  Cause: the MOS saves a byte by sharing it between two errors:

  E310: 00 FE "Bad command"    ← brk, error number, message
  E31D: 00                     ← ends "Bad command" AND is the brk of the next 
  error
  E31E: FB "Bad key" 00

  The tracer reached $E310 first and marked its whole error block as data,
  including the $00 at $E31D. When the branches at $E32A and $E32E later reached
  $E31D, the tracer only handles a brk on a byte not yet classified. So it left
  $E31D alone, and it showed as a bare dta $00 with "Bad key" as plain bytes.

  Fix (js/core.js): the tracer now remembers which zeros it marked only as the
  end of an error block. A later brk there claims the byte. Marking an error
  block also skips bytes already traced as code, so the result doesn't depend on
  which error is traced first. Ransack now reads:

  lE310
      brk
      dta $FE,c'Bad command'
  lE31D
      brk
      dta $FB,c'Bad key',$00

  Tests: all 88 round-trip cases and 169 UI checks pass. The new round-trip case
  has two chained errors sharing a zero, with the second reached by a branch;
  it fails without the fix.

  edits again?

❯ How should we deal with the symbol additions? Add them to the harvest script  
  as hardcodes? Is it possible to make BBC's NMIVEC symbol defined but disabled 
  by default?

● Yes to both. Here's what I'd do.

  1. Put the additions in the harvest script. bbchw.dop and bbcmos.dop are
  generated by tools/harvest-bbc.py, so edits to them are lost the next time it
  runs. I'd add a small hand-written block to the script, commented as not
  coming from py8dis or the MOS reassembly:
  - the three 6502 vectors in bbchw.dop, under a "6502 VECTORS" heading;
  - your two ROM header changes in bbcmos.dop.

  Then tools/embed-symbols.py rebuilds js/symbols.js as usual. Your bbchw.dop
  now has vector IRQVEC, so the earlier ggvector typo is already gone.

  2. ROM header as code: your change suits Ransack, where the dump has a
  sideways ROM paged in at $8000. But bbcmos.dop loads for every BBC project. In
  a game dump where $8000 is RAM or empty, code $8000 would trace garbage. It's
  also only valid for a language ROM; a service-only ROM has no JMP at $8000.
  So these two should be off by default too, which is the same mechanism as
  question 3.

  3. "Defined but off by default" is possible, and close to what we already
  have. Each project's symbol set already keeps a list of switched-off labels
  (inc.off, saved as ;xdis off <set> <names>). A switched-off label is left out
  completely: it isn't traced and doesn't name anything. In the viewer it shows
  unticked, and one click turns it on. What's missing is a way for the set file
  itself to name labels that start off. I'd add a line to the set's .dop:

  vector NMIVEC=$FFFA+1
  vector RSTVEC=$FFFC+1
  vector IRQVEC=$FFFE+1   ; also BRK
  ;xdis defaultoff NMIVEC RSTVEC IRQVEC

  When a set is added to a project, its off list would start with those names.
  For projects that already include the set, a refresh of the built-in sets
  would switch off only labels that are new to it, so choices you've already
  made stay as they are. The dis CLI ignores ;xdis lines, so the files still
  work there.

  Which labels should start off is your call. I'd make it all three vectors plus
  the two ROM entries. NMIVEC points at the $0D00 NMI area, which in a memory
  dump is often just leftover bytes. IRQVEC and RSTVEC only matter for
  disassembling the MOS itself.

  Want me to implement it: the defaultoff line, the harvest-script additions,
  and regenerating the symbol files? That would replace your hand edits with the
  generated equivalents.

● Symbol sets can now name labels that start switched off. Your symbol additions
  are generated by the harvest script, with NMIVEC and the two ROM entries off
  by default. Nothing is committed yet.

  Set files: a symbol set can include a ;xdis defaultoff NAME… line. The dis CLI
  ignores ;xdis lines, so the files still work there.
  - bbchw.dop gets a "6502 VECTORS" section with NMIVEC, RSTVEC and IRQVEC
    (commented "also BRK"), and ;xdis defaultoff NMIVEC.
  - bbcmos.dop has romStartAddress and romServiceEntry as code, as you'd edited
    them, with ;xdis defaultoff romStartAddress romServiceEntry. Without that,
    code $8000 would trace garbage in BBC dumps where $8000 isn't a ROM.

  Harvest script: these additions are in a short hand-written block at the top
  of tools/harvest-bbc.py, with the reasons, so regenerating keeps them. I
  regenerated both files and js/symbols.js. Apart from the defaultoff lines and
  one comment line above each, the output matches your hand edits. Your editor
  backups (*.dop~) are untouched.

  How it behaves:
  - Adding a set to a project starts its default-off labels off, everywhere sets
    get added. Before you've added a set, its viewer already shows those labels
    unticked.
  - Existing projects pick this up when the built-in sets update. Labels that
    just became default-off are switched off, including in projects saved with
    your hand-edited files. Labels already default-off in the project's copy
    keep whatever setting you chose. So your Ransack projects will now open with
    NMIVEC and the two ROM entries off, and you can tick any of them back on.
  - .dop export and import: an exported .dop now always writes the ;xdis off 
    <set> line for a set that has default-off labels, even when the list is
    empty. Importing replaces the set's list rather than adding to it. So a
    label you switched on stays on through export and import.

  Tests: all 90 round-trip cases pass. The two new ones check that NMIVEC's
  handler isn't traced by default while IRQVEC's and RSTVEC's are, and that it
  is once switched on. The round-trip harness now applies default-off labels the
  way the app does. The UI suite passes all 172 checks in 3 out of 3 runs. The
  three new checks cover the viewer showing NMIVEC unticked before the set is
  used, adding the set starting it off, and undo. I also checked the refresh
  rules and the .dop round trip directly with a script. The README documents
  defaultoff and the BBC defaults.

  Want me to commit it? This time that would include your symbol files (now
  generated), plus README.md, js/app.js, js/core.js, js/symbols.js, both tests
  and tools/harvest-bbc.py. The backup files and ransack-main.asm would stay
  out.

❯ Can you help me brainstorm how to deal with constants? I don't like how dis   
  -C worked where it replaced all uses of a value across the board. I guess we  
  should support defining enums and assigning individual instructions to one    
  (or more?) of those enum classes?                                             

● Agreed. A global value-to-name mapping is the wrong default: #$00 is a colour
  in one place, a loop counter in the next, and a zero high byte in a third.
  Today xdis copies dis exactly. A constant NAME=$XX names that byte in every
  immediate operand, apart from the ones shown as #</#> address halves.

  Here's how I'd think about the alternatives.

  1. Enums as named groups of values

  An enum is a named set of members, each a name and a value:

  ;xdis enum color   BLACK=$00 WHITE=$01 RED=$02 CYAN=$03
  ;xdis enum state   IDLE=0 RUNNING=1 DEAD=2

  The output gets an equate block per enum that's actually used:

  ; color
  BLACK   equ $00
  RED     equ $02

  A value with no member in the chosen enum stays a number. That's a useful
  signal: it may be a missing member, or the operand isn't really that enum.

  2. Where an enum applies: four scopes, from explicit to inferred

  a. One instruction. ;xdis enumop $2034 color. This is the precise,
  always-correct building block. Assigning an instruction to more than one enum
  doesn't make sense, since an operand has one meaning. More than one should
  only happen as a conflict between inferred scopes (see below).

  b. A variable or register. This is the big win. Tag a memory location once,
  ;xdis enumvar PLAYER_STATE state, and it applies to:
  - lda #2 / sta PLAYER_STATE (and ldx/stx, ldy/sty);
  - lda PLAYER_STATE / cmp #2, and ldx with cpx;
  - lda PLAYER_STATE,x / cmp #2, for a table of states.

  The tracer already follows known immediates in registers for bank switching,
  and the pointer-pair detector does the same "lda # … sta P" matching. So this
  is a modest amount of new work. Hardware registers are the same case: DMACTL,
  NMIEN, C64 $D011 and the BBC's ROMSEL would each get an enum.

  c. A routine's register parameter. ;xdis enumreg OSBYTE a osbyte: the A loaded
  before jsr OSBYTE is an OSBYTE call number. The same idea works for your own
  routines (lda #SND_EXPLODE / jsr playsound). The inline work used the same
  kind of per-routine convention.

  d. A data table. ;xdis enumdata $3000+1F state makes dta $00,$01 read dta 
  IDLE,RUNNING.

  Precedence: one instruction, then variable, then routine parameter, then the
  old global constant. When two inferred scopes disagree, the operand shows both
  in its inspector panel and you pick one, which creates an enumop.

  3. Bit-flag enums

  Many hardware values are flag sets, not single values. An enum can be marked
  flags:

  ;xdis enum dmactl flags NARROW=$01 NORMAL=$02 MISSILES=$04 PLAYERS=$08 
  ONELINE=$10 DL=$20

  lda #$2E / sta DMACTL then becomes lda #DL|PLAYERS|MISSILES|NORMAL. and #$DF
  could show as and #~DL, but xasm and MADS treat ~ differently, so the safer
  form is and #$FF^DL. Any leftover bits stay as a number: #DL|$40.

  4. Built-in enums in the symbol sets

  The hardware sets could ship enums for their registers, with the enumvar
  already attached: Atari DMACTL/NMIEN/GRACTL/PRIOR, C64 VIC control registers,
  BBC OSBYTE and OSWORD numbers and VIA bits. They'd be off by default where
  they might surprise people, using the defaultoff mechanism we just added.

  5. UI

  - Inspector: for an immediate or a stored variable, show the enum it gets and
    where from (instruction, variable or routine). A picker sets or overrides
    it, and you can add a member for this value on the spot. That's K, reworked:
    "name this value in enum…".
  - An Enums panel: each enum with its members, use counts, and the variables,
    routines and tables it's attached to.
  - Suggestions: "#$02 is stored into PLAYER_STATE, which has enum state — apply
    to 14 instructions?". This fits the existing suggestion flow.

  6. Compatibility

  - The constant directive keeps working as dis does, so imported dis .dop files
    still work. I'd stop promoting it in the UI.
  - The new directives are ;xdis lines, so the dis CLI ignores them.
  - Projects already using constant could be offered "convert to an enum
    attached to its uses". That's a one-time migration.

  Suggested phases

  1. Enums with members, per-instruction assignment, the inspector picker and
     the equate output. This is small, and replaces -C usefully on its own.
  2. Variable, register and routine-parameter scopes with inference, and
     conflict display.
  3. Flag enums, then built-in enums for the hardware and OS registers.

  Two decisions for you:
  - Should values with no matching member in the chosen enum stay as plain
    numbers (my preference), or be flagged in Problems?
  - How much should variable-scope inference cover? Just lda #/sta VAR and lda 
    VAR/cmp # in straight-line code is cheap and predictable. Following values
    through other registers and across branches catches more, but is harder to
    predict.

● Phase 1 of enums is in place, and values an enum doesn't name stay as plain
  numbers. Nothing is committed yet.

  Directives (;xdis lines in .dop files, so the dis CLI ignores them):

  ;xdis enum color BLACK=$00 WHITE=$01 RED=$02
  ;xdis enumop $2034 color

  - enum NAME MEMBER=$XX … defines a set of byte values. Values are hex, as
    elsewhere in .dop files. Several enum lines with the same name merge.
  - enumop [seg:]$ADDR NAME makes the immediate operand of that one instruction
    a value of the enum. It takes priority over #</#> address halves and over a
    global constant.

  Output:
  BLACK equ $00                 ; enum color
  WHITE equ $01
  RED equ $02
  ...
      lda #RED                  ; 080D: A9 02
      lda #DEAD                 ; 0812: A9 02   (same value, different enum)
      cmp #$07                  ; 0816: C9 07   (state has no member for 7)
      ldx #$02                  ; 081A: A2 02   (no enum: untouched)
  Every member of an enum that's used anywhere gets an equate, so the whole set
  is documented. An operand override (O) that names a member also counts as a
  use. If the same member name has different values in two enums, it's reported
  in Problems.

  UI:
  - E (also in the right-click menu) opens a dialog to pick the operand's enum
    or type a new name, and to name the value in it. Leaving the enum empty
    removes it from this instruction.
  - The inspector for an immediate shows "Enum for this operand", with none, the
    existing enums and New enum…. Under it is an editable field for the value's
    name in that enum.
  - K still sets a global constant. Its label now says "(every use, like dis
    -C)" so the difference is clear.

  Tests: all 93 round-trip cases pass. The two new ones (xasm and MADS) check
  the cases above and reassemble byte-identically. The UI suite passes all 180
  checks in 2 out of 2 runs. Eight new checks cover the E dialog creating the
  enum and member, the operand and equates, other uses staying untouched, the
  inspector picker, choosing none, and undo. I added a README section and help
  entries.

❯ Could you give me some example enum values I could use for OSBYTE?            

● Here's a ready-to-paste set based on the OSBYTE calls in Acorn's Advanced User
  Guide. Several enum lines with the same name merge, so it's split into
  groups. Values are hex, so $8C is OSBYTE &8C (140, *TAPE).

  ; OSBYTE call numbers (A on entry); *FXn is OSBYTE n
  ;xdis enum osbyte OSB_OSVERSION=$00 OSB_USERFLAG=$01 OSB_INPUTSTREAM=$02 
  OSB_OUTPUTSTREAMS=$03 OSB_CURSORKEYS=$04
  ;xdis enum osbyte OSB_PRINTERTYPE=$05 OSB_PRINTERIGNORE=$06 OSB_RXBAUD=$07 
  OSB_TXBAUD=$08 OSB_FLASHMARK=$09 OSB_FLASHSPACE=$0A
  ;xdis enum osbyte OSB_REPEATDELAY=$0B OSB_REPEATPERIOD=$0C 
  OSB_DISABLEEVENT=$0D OSB_ENABLEEVENT=$0E OSB_FLUSHBUFFERS=$0F
  ;xdis enum osbyte OSB_ADCCHANNELS=$10 OSB_STARTADC=$11 OSB_RESETSOFTKEYS=$12 
  OSB_WAITVSYNC=$13 OSB_EXPLODEFONT=$14 OSB_FLUSHBUFFER=$15
  ;xdis enum osbyte OSB_READVDUSTATUS=$75 OSB_KEYBOARDLEDS=$76 
  OSB_CLOSESPOOLEXEC=$77 OSB_WRITEKEYS=$78 OSB_KEYSCAN=$79 OSB_KEYSCAN16=$7A
  ;xdis enum osbyte OSB_PRINTERDORMANT=$7B OSB_CLEARESCAPE=$7C OSB_SETESCAPE=$7D
  OSB_ACKESCAPE=$7E OSB_EOF=$7F
  ;xdis enum osbyte OSB_ADCORBUFFER=$80 OSB_INKEY=$81 OSB_HIGHORDERADDR=$82 
  OSB_READOSHWM=$83 OSB_READHIMEM=$84 OSB_MODEHIMEM=$85
  ;xdis enum osbyte OSB_CURSORPOS=$86 OSB_CHARATCURSOR=$87 OSB_CODE=$88 
  OSB_MOTOR=$89 OSB_INSERTBUFFER=$8A OSB_OPT=$8B
  ;xdis enum osbyte OSB_TAPE=$8C OSB_ROMFS=$8D OSB_ENTERLANGUAGE=$8E 
  OSB_SERVICECALL=$8F OSB_TV=$90 OSB_GETFROMBUFFER=$91
  ;xdis enum osbyte OSB_READFRED=$92 OSB_WRITEFRED=$93 OSB_READJIM=$94 
  OSB_WRITEJIM=$95 OSB_READSHEILA=$96 OSB_WRITESHEILA=$97
  ;xdis enum osbyte OSB_BUFFERSTATUS=$98 OSB_INSERTINPUT=$99 
  OSB_VIDEOULACTRL=$9A OSB_VIDEOULAPALETTE=$9B OSB_ACIACTRL=$9C
  ;xdis enum osbyte OSB_FASTBPUT=$9D OSB_READSPEECH=$9E OSB_WRITESPEECH=$9F 
  OSB_READVDUVAR=$A0
  ;xdis enum osbyte OSB_BREAKESCAPE=$C8 OSB_KEYBOARDDISABLE=$C9 
  OSB_KEYBOARDSTATUS=$CA OSB_SOUNDSUPPRESS=$D2 OSB_VDUQUEUE=$DA
  ;xdis enum osbyte OSB_ESCAPECHAR=$DC OSB_ESCAPEKEY=$E5 OSB_ESCAPEEFFECTS=$E6 
  OSB_CHARDESTINATION=$EC OSB_STARTUPOPTIONS=$FF

  Three of these come up in the Ransack code we've looked at:
  - lda #$C8 / ldx #3 / jsr OSBYTE is *FX200,3: ESCAPE disabled, and BREAK
    clears memory. That gives lda #OSB_BREAKESCAPE.
  - lda #$8C / … / jsr OSBYTE selects the cassette filing system (*TAPE): lda 
    #OSB_TAPE.
  - lda #$99 / jmp OSBYTE inserts a character into the input buffer: lda 
    #OSB_INSERTINPUT.

  Some notes:
  - Names: these are my own names, made from the Guide's descriptions. Acorn
    didn't define official symbols for OSBYTE numbers; people mostly wrote *FX
    numbers. The OSB_ prefix keeps them from clashing with labels like OSBYTE or
    the MOS workspace names in bbcmos.dop.
  - Coverage: the range from $A6 up holds the "read/write OS variable" calls,
    and I've only listed the common ones. The full table runs to $FF, so add
    more as you meet them.
  - Accuracy: I wrote this list from memory of the Guide, so double-check any
    entry you rely on, especially in the $A6–$FF range.

❯ What does A=$B6 mean to OSBYTE?                                               

  Searched for 2 patterns (ctrl+o to expand)

● The cached MOS 1.20 reassembly has the workspace names. OSBYTE &A6 and up read
  and write OS variables, so I'll look up which variable &B6 maps to:

  Ran 2 shell commands (ctrl+o to expand)

● On a BBC Micro with MOS 1.20, OSBYTE &B6 (182) reads the font explosion state.
  That's the value of X last given to *FX20 (OSBYTE 20): which ranges of
  characters currently have redefinable (soft) definitions in RAM.

  I got this from the MOS 1.20 reassembly cached for the harvest script:
  - Calls from &A6 up read or write the OS variables in $0236–$02FF. Each call's
    variable is at $0236 + (A − &A6).
  - For &B6 that's $0246, which the reassembly calls
    softCharacterDefinitionsSwitch ("the value X used in *FX 20,X").
  - It's listed as read-only. Read it the usual way for these calls, with X=0, 
    Y=&FF (the new value is (old AND Y) EOR X); the result comes back in X.
  - The reassembly warns that 182 means something different on the Master 
    series, so code meant for both machines shouldn't rely on it.

  It isn't in the enum list I gave you, which skipped most of the &A6–&FF range.
  A matching member would be OSB_FONTEXPLOSION=$B6.
